title: Multi-Agent Systems

techniques.name: Single vs Multi-Agent
techniques.q: Should I split this across agents at all?
techniques.what: A decision method, not a framework. Split work across agents only when the pieces are independent enough to run in parallel and too big for one context window. Parallel agents cut wall time and add coverage, but they multiply tokens: Anthropic reports agents using about 4× the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15×. Otherwise one agent is cheaper and more coherent.
use: Research across many independent sources, such as 12 companies’ results
Material too large for one context window when read together
Deadlines where saved minutes are worth more than extra tokens
metrics: subtasks that share no inputs can run at once
each branch must fit one window; the whole job may not
about 4× chat for one agent, about 15× for multi-agent (Anthropic)
parallel time is the slowest branch plus merging, not the sum
coupled decisions split across agents can conflict (Cognition)
split only if time or coverage gained is worth more than the extra tokens
steps: Write the job as a small task graph with the inputs each step needs
Count branches that share no inputs, and check each fits one context window
Estimate tokens (about 4× vs 15× a chat baseline) and wall time for both designs
Price both, including the value of time saved, and split only if multi-agent wins
pitfalls: Splitting coupled work: agents make conflicting implicit decisions
Forgetting that parallelism saves time, not tokens
Coding and shared-context tasks rarely have enough truly parallel pieces
techniques.remember: Split for breadth, not by default. Parallel saves minutes, not tokens.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 6 minutes and about 2k chat-equivalent tokens per filing (10k in all); 4× that for one agent (40k) and 15× for five (150k), plus 1 minute to merge.

cmp.needs: A task graph and a cost estimate

techniques.name: Supervisor and Workers
techniques.q: Who splits the job and puts it back together?
techniques.what: An orchestrator breaks a task into pieces and sends each to a worker sub-agent. Each worker starts with a fresh context, its own brief and a restricted set of tools, and returns only a short final message, so the orchestrator’s context stays clean. The orchestrator then merges the results and flags gaps. Anthropic calls this the orchestrator–workers pattern.
use: Research or review that splits into independent parts
Work where each part needs different tools or permissions
Long jobs where one context would overflow with raw material
metrics: plans, delegates at run time and synthesizes
objective, output format, sources and task boundaries
a worker sees only its own prompt and the brief it is given
only the worker’s final message reaches the orchestrator
least privilege per worker, for example Read and Grep only
Claude Agent SDK: nesting depth 3 and 20 concurrent sub-agents by default
steps: Define each worker with a description, a system prompt and a minimal tool list
Write every brief so it carries all the context a fresh worker needs
Fan the workers out concurrently, with a budget or concurrency cap
Ask for a fixed, compact output format, then merge and list what is missing
pitfalls: Vague briefs make workers duplicate each other or wander out of scope
Returning full transcripts floods the orchestrator’s context
Spawning many workers for a simple question burns tokens for nothing
techniques.remember: Brief fully, scope tightly, return summaries.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: four workers each read about 30k tokens and return about 1k; the orchestrator holds 2k of its own plus 4k of summaries.

techniques.name: Handoffs
techniques.q: Who should own the conversation now?
techniques.what: One agent transfers the live conversation to a specialist, who then answers the user directly. A supervisor keeps control; a handoff gives it away. Handoffs are exposed to the model as tools, such as transfer_to_card_agent in the OpenAI Agents SDK, so routing depends on their names and descriptions. What history travels with the handoff decides whether the user must repeat themselves.
use: Support bots with distinct specialist areas: cards, loans, fraud
Conversations whose owner should change midway
Specialists that need their own tools, permissions or instructions
metrics: the triage model routes on them, so make them distinct
structured payload the model fills in on handoff
trims what history the specialist sees
caps the loop; exceeding it raises MaxTurnsExceeded
the specialist owns the rest of the turn
steps: Build specialists with narrow, non-overlapping responsibilities
Write handoff descriptions that say exactly when to transfer
Pass the facts the specialist needs as a typed payload, not the whole transcript
Cap turns, and allow hand-backs only with a limit on hops
pitfalls: Overlapping descriptions cause misroutes and ping-pong
Passing no context makes users repeat themselves
Peer-to-peer handoffs without caps can loop
techniques.remember: Distinct descriptions, typed payloads, capped hops.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a 3-field payload replaces 14 messages of history, and the user no longer has to repeat details.

techniques.name: Shared State vs Message Passing
techniques.q: How do agents know what the others found?
techniques.what: Agents coordinate in one of two ways. They write to a common store, such as a blackboard, scratchpad or typed graph state, or they send each other structured messages. The design choices are who writes which fields, how concurrent writes merge, how much each agent reads, and whether every entry records who wrote it and from which source.
use: Several agents contributing findings to one decision
Parallel writers that must not overwrite each other
Audited work where every claim needs a source
metrics: one typed store every agent can read (blackboard)
how updates merge; with none, a key is overwritten
typed messages sent to named recipients
each agent reads only the fields it needs
who wrote each entry and from which source
an open protocol for messages between separate agent systems
steps: Type the state: findings, open questions, decisions
Give every multi-writer field a reducer such as operator.add
Scope reads so each agent loads only what it needs
Record the author and source on every entry
pitfalls: A key with no reducer loses parallel writes
Everyone reading everything multiplies tokens
Free-text chat buries findings and drops sources
techniques.remember: Type it, reduce it, scope it, source it.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: writers produce 4, 3 and 5 findings of about 0.75k tokens each.

techniques.name: Debate and Critic Ensembles
techniques.q: Will more opinions make the answer more correct?
techniques.what: Several agents answer independently, read each other’s reasoning over a few rounds, and settle on an answer by vote or by a judge. It costs a multiple of a single call. Du et al. (2023) reported gains with 3 agents and 2 rounds, but later work found that majority voting accounts for most of those gains, so debate is worth it only when agents’ errors are independent and a second opinion can catch them.
use: High-stakes answers where errors are costly: coverage, compliance, diagnosis support
Questions with a checkable argument that others can verify
Deciding which cases to escalate: disagreement is a useful signal
metrics: one agent anchors on its first answer (Liang et al.)
settles a split; may be unfair across different models
debate does not reliably beat self-consistency
majority voting explains most of debate’s gains
steps: Collect independent first answers, ideally from varied prompts or models
Share answers and reasons for one or two rounds; stop early on agreement
Aggregate by majority vote or a judge with a rubric, never the last speaker
Compare against plain voting at the same cost before adopting debate
pitfalls: Correlated agents agree on the same mistake
Agents conform to a confident but wrong peer
Rounds multiply cost for little gain over voting
techniques.remember: Vote first. Debate only if it beats the vote.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 3 agents × 3 rounds = 9 calls; plain voting uses 3.

techniques.name: Failure Modes and Coordination Control
techniques.q: Why did the team loop, stall or overspend?
techniques.what: Multi-agent teams repeat steps, miss stopping conditions, ignore each other, stop early or skip verification. The MAST study of over 1,600 traces sorts these into 14 modes in three categories. Coordination control answers them with hard caps on turns, tokens, time and depth, combined so that any one can stop the run, plus explicit stop signals, repetition detection and a verifier.
use: Any agent team that runs unattended: overnight, in CI, at scale
Coder–reviewer or peer-to-peer loops
Budgets that must hold per run or per day
metrics: system design ≈ 44%, inter-agent misalignment ≈ 32%, task verification ≈ 24%
step repetition 15.7%, reasoning–action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of stopping 12.4%
max_budget_usd ends the run and refuses new sub-agents
GraphRecursionError at the recursion limit (1000 by default from v1.0.6)
steps: Name one explicit stop signal, such as TERMINATE, and say when to use it
Add caps on messages, tokens and time, combined with OR
Detect repeated messages and intervene before the loop runs on
Verify with a real check before accepting done; return partial results with a reason
pitfalls: Combining caps with AND means none fires until all do
Caps set too tight cut legitimate long runs
A done claim without a check ships wrong output
techniques.remember: Any cap stops it. Nothing counts as done until checked.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 4k tokens per message. Repetition is caught at message 9 and tests pass at message 12.

cmp.needs: Caps, a stop signal and a verifier

techniques.name: Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context
techniques.q: How do I run many pieces at once without flooding one context?
techniques.what: An orchestrator splits a job into independent pieces and starts one sub-agent per piece, all at the same time. Each sub-agent gets a fresh, isolated context window holding only its brief, does its own reading and tool calls, and returns a condensed result, such as a card of at most 500 tokens, instead of its transcript. Anthropic’s multi-agent research system works this way. This page covers the fan-out and fan-in mechanics: concurrency, condensed returns, shared inputs and the merge check. Whether to split at all is Single vs Multi-Agent; how workers are briefed and tool-scoped is Supervisor and Workers.
use: Comparing many independent entities at once, such as 12 companies’ quarterly results
Broad research across sources that together overflow one context window
Batch reviews where each item can be judged on its own: loan files, claims, contracts
metrics: one sub-agent per independent piece, started together under a concurrency cap
each sub-agent sees its brief and its own tool results, nothing else
a fixed schema of at most about 500 tokens per item, not the transcript
the slowest sub-agent plus planning and merging, not the sum of all
every sub-agent pays its own prompt, tools and reasoning, so the total rises with fan-out
the fan-in step that compares shared figures, units and gaps before synthesis
steps: Split the job into pieces that share no inputs; compute any shared input once and put it in every brief
Start one fresh session per piece, all at once, under a concurrency and budget cap
Have each return a validated card of at most about 500 tokens, with its sources
Fan in through a merge check: same shared figures, same units, no gaps, conflicts flagged
pitfalls: Each sub-agent re-derives a shared input, so work is duplicated and findings conflict
Returning transcripts refills the orchestrator’s context that isolation was meant to protect
Awaiting sub-agents one by one in a loop quietly makes the fan-out sequential
techniques.remember: Fan out the independent, pass shared inputs in, bring back cards, check before merging.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 12 pharma companies at Dalal Lens Research, a fictional equity-research firm; 40k tokens of filings each, 40k of overhead per sub-agent, a 200k window, ₹0.40 per 1,000 tokens.

cmp.needs: Independent pieces and a return schema

whenmulti.code:
TASKS = {                                   # task -> inputs it needs   #@1
    "read_TCS": [], "read_INFY": [], "read_HDFCB": [],               #@1
    "read_ITC": [], "read_LT": [],                                   #@1
    "valuation": ["read_TCS", "read_INFY", "read_HDFCB",             #@1
                  "read_ITC", "read_LT"],                            #@1
}
MINUTES = {t: 6 for t in TASKS}                                      #@5
BASE_TOKENS = 2_000                  # chat-equivalent, per filing    #@4
WINDOW = 200_000                     # one context window             #@3
INR_PER_MIN, INR_PER_1K = 20, 0.5                                    #@6

branches = [t for t, needs in TASKS.items() if not needs]            #@2
coupled = [t for t, needs in TASKS.items() if needs]  # keep together #@2

per_branch = 4 * BASE_TOKENS                                         #@3
fits = per_branch < WINDOW                                           #@3

single_tokens = 4 * BASE_TOKENS * len(branches)       # 40k          #@4
multi_tokens = 15 * BASE_TOKENS * len(branches)       # 150k         #@4

single_min = sum(MINUTES[t] for t in branches)        # 30           #@5
multi_min = max(MINUTES[t] for t in branches) + 1     # 7, with merge #@5

saved = (single_min - multi_min) * INR_PER_MIN                       #@6
extra = (multi_tokens - single_tokens) / 1000 * INR_PER_1K           #@6
split = len(branches) > 1 and fits and saved > extra                 #@6
print(split, saved, extra)            # True 460 55.0                #@6
steps: Sketch the dependencies
Write the job as a small task graph: each task and the inputs it needs. Five filings can each be read alone; the valuation needs all five.
Count independent branches
Tasks that need nothing from each other can run at the same time. Here there are 5 such branches; the coupled valuation stays with one agent.
Check context per branch
Each branch must fit in one context window. One filing needs about 8k tokens of working context, far below 200k.
Estimate tokens
Agents use about 4× the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15×, so 10k of chat-equivalent work becomes about 40k for one agent and 150k for five.
Estimate wall time
Parallel time is the slowest branch plus merging, not the sum: 6 + 1 = 7 minutes, against 30 minutes one after another.
Decide
Split only if what the time saves is worth more than the extra tokens. At INR 20 a minute, 23 minutes saved is worth INR 460 against INR 55 of extra tokens.

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

CLASSES = ["SGLT2", "DPP-4", "statins", "ARBs"]                    #@1
BRIEF = """Objective: list suspected adverse events for {c} drugs.  #@3
Output: JSON rows {{drug, event, paper_id, quote}}, at most 40.     #@3
Sources: only files under ./papers/{c}/. No web search.            #@3
Boundaries: do not judge causality. Stop when every file is read.""" #@3

workers = {
    f"screen-{c.lower()}": AgentDefinition(                        #@1
        description=f"Screens {c} papers for adverse events.",     #@1
        prompt=BRIEF.format(c=c),              # the whole brief    #@1,3
        tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],        # read-only worker   #@2
        model="sonnet",                                            #@1
    )
    for c in CLASSES
}

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Agent"],               #@4
    agents=workers,                                                #@4
    max_budget_usd=5.0,                # caps sub-agents as well    #@4
)

PLAN = ("Run the four screeners in parallel. Each returns only "   #@4,5
        "its JSON rows. Merge them into one table, remove "        #@6
        "duplicates and list any paper no worker could read.")     #@6

async def main():
    async for msg in query(prompt=PLAN, options=options):          #@4
        if hasattr(msg, "result"):     # final message only         #@5
            print(msg.result)          # merged table and gaps      #@6
steps: Define the workers
One sub-agent per drug class, each with a description (when to use it), a system prompt and a model.
Restrict tools
Screeners only read, so they get Read, Grep and Glob. A worker that cannot write cannot damage shared files.
Write the brief
A worker starts with a fresh context and sees only its own prompt, so the brief carries everything: objective, output format, sources and boundaries.
Fan out
The orchestrator calls the four workers through the Agent tool and they run at the same time, under one spend cap for the whole query.
Collect summaries
Each worker read about 30k tokens, but only its final message returns: about 1k each. The orchestrator holds about 6k, not 122k.
Synthesize
The orchestrator merges the rows, removes duplicates and lists what is missing, so a human reviewer sees both the findings and the gaps.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from pydantic import BaseModel
from agents import Agent, Runner, RunContextWrapper, handoff
from agents.extensions import handoff_filters

class CardCase(BaseModel):                                          #@4
    card_last4: str                                                 #@4
    reason: str                                                     #@4

@dataclass
class Chat:
    case: CardCase | None = None                                    #@4

async def keep_case(ctx: RunContextWrapper[Chat], case: CardCase):  #@4
    ctx.context.case = case                # the typed payload       #@4

card = Agent[Chat](name="Card agent",                               #@1
    instructions=lambda ctx, a: f"Resolve this case: {ctx.context.case}",   #@1,4
    handoff_description="Blocked or declined debit and credit cards.")      #@2
loan = Agent[Chat](name="Loan agent", instructions="Resolve loan EMIs.",    #@1
    handoff_description="Loan EMIs, bounced EMIs and foreclosure.")        #@2
fraud = Agent[Chat](name="Fraud agent", instructions="Freeze and report.", #@1
    handoff_description="Transactions the customer does not recognise.")   #@2

triage = Agent[Chat](name="Triage",                                 #@3
    instructions="Decide which specialist owns this, then hand off.",       #@3
    handoffs=[handoff(card, input_type=CardCase, on_handoff=keep_case,      #@3,4
                      input_filter=handoff_filters.remove_all_tools),       #@5
              loan, fraud])                                         #@3

result = Runner.run_sync(triage, "EMI bounced, card blocked?",      #@6
                         context=Chat(), max_turns=8)               #@6
print(result.last_agent.name)             # Card agent              #@6
steps: Build specialists
Three agents, each owning one area: cards, loans and fraud. Each has its own instructions and could have its own tools and permissions.
Write distinct descriptions
Handoffs reach the model as tools named transfer_to_card_agent and so on. The triage model routes on these descriptions, so they must not overlap.
Attach them to triage
handoffs=[...] gives triage one transfer tool per specialist. Triage only decides who owns the chat; it does not answer.
Pass a typed payload
input_type makes the model fill in a CardCase (last four digits and reason) when it hands off, and on_handoff stores it where the card agent’s instructions can read it.
Trim the history
input_filter removes earlier tool calls from what the card agent sees. It gets the conversation and the payload, not every intermediate step.
Cap the turns
max_turns bounds the whole run; going past it raises MaxTurnsExceeded. The card agent now owns the chat and resolves it in 2 turns.

import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

class Entry(TypedDict):                                            #@1,5
    text: str                                                      #@1
    agent: str                                                     #@5
    source: str                                                    #@5

class Board(TypedDict):                                            #@1
    findings: Annotated[list[Entry], operator.add]    # append      #@1,2
    questions: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]     # append      #@1,2
    decision: str                                     # one writer  #@1,2

def carrier(s: Board):                                             #@3
    return {"findings": [Entry(text="Linehaul delayed 18 h",       #@3
            agent="carrier", source="carrier API #A71")]}          #@5
def weather(s: Board):                                             #@3
    return {"findings": [Entry(text="Rain alert, Nagpur",          #@3
            agent="weather", source="IMD bulletin 14:00")]}        #@5
def dispatcher(s: Board):                    # reads findings only  #@4
    risks = [f for f in s["findings"] if f["agent"] in ("carrier", "weather")]   #@4
    return {"decision": "reroute" if len(risks) >= 2 else "hold"}  #@4

g = StateGraph(Board)
for name, fn in [("carrier", carrier), ("weather", weather), ("dispatcher", dispatcher)]:
    g.add_node(name, fn)
g.add_edge(START, "carrier"); g.add_edge(START, "weather")         #@3
g.add_edge(["carrier", "weather"], "dispatcher")      # join         #@3,4
g.add_edge("dispatcher", END)
print(g.compile().invoke({"findings": [], "questions": []}))

@dataclass
class Msg:                           # the same flow as typed messages  #@6
    sender: str; to: str; data: dict; source: str                  #@6
note = Msg("carrier", "dispatcher", {"delay_h": 18}, "carrier API #A71")   #@6
steps: Type the state
The board is a typed dict with three fields: findings, open questions and the decision. Every finding is an Entry, not free text.
Choose a reducer per field
findings and questions use operator.add, so parallel updates are appended. decision has one writer, so plain replacement is safe.
Fan out parallel writers
The carrier and weather agents start together from START and each returns one finding. Without the reducer, LangGraph would reject the two same-step writes with InvalidUpdateError.
Scope reads
The dispatcher reads only the findings it needs and writes only the decision. Smaller reads mean fewer tokens and less distraction.
Record provenance
Every entry names the agent that wrote it and its source, so a reviewer can trace the reroute decision back to the carrier API and the IMD bulletin.
Contrast with messages
The same flow can run as typed messages sent to a named recipient. Each agent then sees only what is addressed to it; protocols such as A2A standardise this across systems.

import asyncio
from collections import Counter

def label(answer: str) -> str:
    return "NOT COVERED" if answer.upper().startswith("NOT") else "COVERED"

async def ask(agent, question, peers=None):           # any chat client
    prompt = question if peers is None else (
        f"{question}\nOther assessors said:\n{peers}\nRevise or defend.")   #@2,3
    return await agent.complete(prompt)

async def debate(agents, question, max_rounds=2):
    answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(a, question) for a in agents))   #@1
    calls = len(agents)                                              #@1
    for _ in range(max_rounds):                                      #@4
        if len({label(x) for x in answers}) == 1:                    #@4
            break                            # all agree: stop early  #@4
        peers = "\n---\n".join(answers)                             #@2
        answers = await asyncio.gather(                              #@3
            *(ask(a, question, peers) for a in agents))              #@3
        calls += len(agents)                                         #@3
    votes = Counter(label(x) for x in answers)                       #@5
    return votes.most_common(1)[0][0], calls         # never answers[-1]   #@5

async def vote_only(agents, question):               # the baseline  #@6
    answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(a, question) for a in agents))   #@6
    return Counter(label(x) for x in answers).most_common(1)[0][0], len(agents)   #@6
steps: Independent first answers
Three agents read the claim and the policy separately. Two say covered, citing the day-care clause; one says not covered.
Share answers and reasons
Each agent now sees the others’ answers and the clauses they relied on. This is where a checkable argument can correct an error.
Revise or defend
Each agent answers again. The third agent finds the day-care clause it missed and changes its answer.
Stop early on agreement
All three now agree, so the second round is skipped. Stopping early saves a third of the calls.
Aggregate the group
The final answer is the majority of the last round, not whichever agent spoke last. A judge with a rubric is the alternative when votes split.
Compare with plain voting
Round 0 alone was already 2 against 1 for covered. Voting got the same answer in 3 calls instead of 6, so debate must earn its extra cost on cases like this.

from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_agentchat.teams import RoundRobinGroupChat
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import (TextMentionTermination,
    MaxMessageTermination, TokenUsageTermination, TimeoutTermination,
    FunctionalTermination)

done = TextMentionTermination("APPROVED")          # the stop signal  #@1
caps = (MaxMessageTermination(30)                                     #@2,3
        | TokenUsageTermination(max_total_token=100_000)              #@2,3
        | TimeoutTermination(timeout_seconds=720))                    #@2,3

seen = {}
def looping(new_msgs) -> bool:           # called with new messages   #@4
    for m in new_msgs:                                                #@4
        if seen.get(m.source) == m.to_text():                        #@4
            return True                  # same text twice in a row   #@4
        seen[m.source] = m.to_text()                                  #@4
    return False

# coder, model and run_tests are defined as usual
reviewer = AssistantAgent("reviewer", model_client=model, tools=[run_tests],   #@5
    system_message="Call run_tests. Say APPROVED only if it returns PASS.")    #@5

stop = done | caps | FunctionalTermination(looping)                  #@3,4
team = RoundRobinGroupChat([coder, reviewer], termination_condition=stop)

async def main():
    result = await team.run(task="Fix the invoice rounding bug")
    if "APPROVED" not in (result.stop_reason or ""):                  #@6
        return {"status": "partial", "reason": result.stop_reason,   #@6
                "last_patch": result.messages[-2].to_text()}          #@6
    return {"status": "done", "patch": result.messages[-2].to_text()}
steps: Name the stop signal
Agree on one explicit word, APPROVED, and say exactly when an agent may use it. Without one, a team has no way to say it is finished.
Add hard caps
Cap messages (30), tokens (100k) and wall time (12 minutes). Agents forget to stop; caps do not.
Combine them with OR
The | operator stops the run when any one condition fires. & would wait until all of them had fired, so a missing stop word could keep it running for ever.
Detect repetition
A custom condition compares each agent’s new message with its previous one. Here the coder resends the same patch at message 9, and the loop is caught.
Verify before stopping
The reviewer must run the tests and may say APPROVED only if they pass. At message 12 they do, so done means checked, not claimed.
Return partial results with a reason
If a cap or the loop check stops the run instead, return the last patch marked partial, with the stop reason, so a person can pick it up.

import asyncio
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage

COMPANIES = ["Arogya", "Sanjivani", "Nilgiri", "Kaveri", "Vindhya", "Tapti",
             "Sahyadri", "Narmada", "Godavari", "Aravalli", "Konkan", "Chambal"]  #@1
SECTOR = {"usd_inr": 86.4, "api_price_index": 112.0}   # computed ONCE, sent to all  #@2

class Card(BaseModel):                     # what comes back: at most ~500 tokens  #@4
    company: str
    revenue_cr: float                      # ₹ crore, one unit for everyone  #@4
    ebitda_margin_pct: float
    usd_inr_used: float                                                  #@6
    red_flags: list[str] = Field(max_length=3)
    sources: list[str]                                                   #@4

BRIEF = """Analyse {co} only, from the files in this folder.
Use these sector figures exactly; do not re-derive them: {sector}
Reply with JSON only, matching this schema, in under 500 tokens: {schema}"""  #@2,4

async def analyse(co: str, sem: asyncio.Semaphore) -> Card:
    async with sem:                                   # at most 6 at once  #@3
        opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
            cwd=f"./filings/{co}",                    # sees only its own folder  #@1
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],
            max_turns=30, max_budget_usd=1.0)                            #@3
        prompt = BRIEF.format(co=co, sector=SECTOR, schema=Card.model_json_schema())
        async for msg in query(prompt=prompt, options=opts):   # new session, fresh context  #@1
            if isinstance(msg, ResultMessage):                           #@4
                return Card.model_validate_json(msg.result)   # the card, not the transcript  #@4
    raise RuntimeError(f"{co}: no result")

async def fan_out(names: list[str]):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(6)                                           #@3
    got = await asyncio.gather(*(analyse(c, sem) for c in names),
                               return_exceptions=True)   # one failure is not all  #@3,5
    cards = {c: r for c, r in zip(names, got) if isinstance(r, Card)}
    return cards, [c for c in names if c not in cards]                   #@5

def merge_check(cards: dict) -> dict:
    rates = {card.usd_inr_used for card in cards.values()}               #@6
    conflicts = [] if rates <= {SECTOR["usd_inr"]} else sorted(rates)    #@6
    return {"cards": list(cards.values()), "conflicts": conflicts}       #@6

async def main():
    cards, missing = await fan_out(COMPANIES)
    if missing:                                                          #@5
        retried, missing = await fan_out(missing)    # retry once, then report  #@5
        cards |= retried                                                 #@5
    return {**merge_check(cards), "missing": missing}                    #@6

report = asyncio.run(main())
steps: One fresh session per company

Every query() call starts a new session with its own context window. The sub-agent for Kaveri sees its brief and the files in ./filings/Kaveri, nothing from the other eleven, and its 40k tokens of filings never leave that session.
Pass shared inputs in, once

All twelve comparisons depend on the same USD/INR rate and API price index. The orchestrator computes them once and writes them into every brief. Left alone, twelve sub-agents would each look them up again: eleven duplicate reads and up to eleven different rates.
Fan out under a cap

asyncio.gather starts all twelve and Semaphore(6) lets six run at a time, so they go in two waves: the wall-clock is about two company-lengths, not twelve. max_turns and max_budget_usd bound each session’s spend.
Return a card, not a transcript

Only the final ResultMessage comes back, validated as a Card of under 500 tokens with its sources. Twelve cards are 6k tokens; twelve transcripts of about 80k each would be 960k, far beyond the orchestrator’s window.
Expect failures
return_exceptions=True means one session that times out or returns bad JSON does not throw away the other eleven. Missing companies are retried once and then reported by name, never silently dropped.
Merge check before synthesis
Fan-in checks that every card used the same USD/INR rate and the same units, and lists conflicts and gaps. The orchestrator then holds about 14k tokens: 2k of its own, 6k of briefs and 6k of cards.

import networkx as nx

G = nx.DiGraph()
for c in ["TCS", "Infosys", "HDFC Bank", "ITC"]:          # 12 in practice
    G.add_node(c, minutes=6, tokens=2_000)                 # chat-equivalent tokens
G.add_node("valuation", minutes=20, tokens=6_000, coupled=True)

def plan(G, merge_min=1):
    work = G.subgraph(n for n in G if not G.nodes[n].get("coupled"))
    branches = list(nx.weakly_connected_components(work))   # share no inputs
    base = sum(d["tokens"] for _, d in work.nodes(data=True))
    t_single = sum(d["minutes"] for _, d in work.nodes(data=True))
    t_multi = max(sum(G.nodes[n]["minutes"] for n in b) for b in branches) + merge_min
    return dict(branches=len(branches),
                single=dict(minutes=t_single, tokens=4 * base),
                multi=dict(minutes=t_multi, tokens=15 * base))

def worth_splitting(p, inr_per_min, inr_per_1k_tokens):
    saved = (p["single"]["minutes"] - p["multi"]["minutes"]) * inr_per_min
    extra = (p["multi"]["tokens"] - p["single"]["tokens"]) / 1000 * inr_per_1k_tokens
    return p["branches"] > 1 and saved > extra

p = plan(G)
print(p, worth_splitting(p, inr_per_min=50, inr_per_1k_tokens=0.5))

CLASSES = ["SGLT2 inhibitors", "DPP-4 inhibitors", "statins", "ARBs"]
BRIEF = ("Screen papers in ./papers/{c} for adverse events. Objective: list every "
         "suspected adverse event linked to a {c} drug. Output: JSON list of "
         "{{drug, event, paper, quote}}. Use only the files given. Do not assess "
         "causality; stop when every file is read.")

agents = {
    c.split()[0].lower(): AgentDefinition(
        description=f"Adverse-event screener for {c}. Use for papers about {c}.",
        prompt=BRIEF.format(c=c),
        tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],          # read-only worker
        model="sonnet",
    ) for c in CLASSES
}

async def main():
    async for msg in query(
        prompt="Run every screener in parallel, then merge their JSON into one "
               "table and list any class with no papers read.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Agent"],
            agents=agents,
            env={"CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH": "1"},   # no nesting
            max_budget_usd=5.0,
        ),
    ):
        if hasattr(msg, "result"):
            print(msg.result)

asyncio.run(main())
supervisor.note: The depth and concurrency limits are environment variables; max_budget_usd caps the whole query, sub-agents included.

import asyncio
from pydantic import BaseModel
from agents import Agent, Runner, RunContextWrapper, handoff
from agents.extensions import handoff_filters

class PortRequest(BaseModel):
    mobile: str
    circle: str
    issue: str

async def log_port(ctx: RunContextWrapper[None], data: PortRequest):
    print("porting handoff:", data.mobile, data.circle)

recharge = Agent(name="Recharge agent",
                 handoff_description="Failed or missing prepaid recharges and plan changes.",
                 instructions="Resolve recharge issues. Never ask again for details you were given.")
porting = Agent(name="Porting agent",
                handoff_description="Moving a number to or from Tarang (MNP), UPC codes.",
                instructions="Resolve porting issues using the payload you receive.")

triage = Agent(
    name="Triage",
    instructions="Classify the problem and hand off. Do not answer it yourself.",
    handoffs=[recharge,
              handoff(porting, input_type=PortRequest, on_handoff=log_port,
                      input_filter=handoff_filters.remove_all_tools)],
)

async def main():
    result = await Runner.run(triage, "My UPC code expired before the port finished",
                              max_turns=8)
    print(result.last_agent.name, "->", result.final_output)

asyncio.run(main())

import asyncio
from collections import Counter
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

client = AsyncOpenAI()
MODEL = "gpt-4.1-mini"                        # use your current model

async def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    r = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.choices[0].message.content

def label(answer: str) -> str:
    return "NOT COVERED" if "NOT COVERED" in answer.upper() else "COVERED"

async def decide(claim: str, policy: str, n=3, rounds=1):
    q = (f"Policy:\n{policy}\n\nClaim:\n{claim}\n\nAnswer COVERED or NOT "
         "COVERED, then quote the clause you rely on.")
    answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(q) for _ in range(n)))
    for _ in range(rounds):
        if len({label(a) for a in answers}) == 1:
            break                              # all agree: stop early
        others = "\n---\n".join(answers)
        answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(
            f"{q}\n\nOther assessors said:\n{others}\n\nRevise or defend "
            "your answer.") for _ in range(n)))
    votes = Counter(label(a) for a in answers)
    verdict, count = votes.most_common(1)[0]
    return verdict if count > n / 2 else "REFER TO ASSESSOR"
debate.note: Always compare with plain majority voting at the same number of calls before adopting debate rounds.

lib: Built-in termination conditions that combine with | (either) and & (both). AutoGen is in maintenance mode; the same pattern exists in Microsoft Agent Framework.
code:
import asyncio, subprocess
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_agentchat.teams import RoundRobinGroupChat
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import (
    TextMentionTermination, MaxMessageTermination, TokenUsageTermination,
    TimeoutTermination, FunctionalTermination)
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient

def run_tests() -> str:
    """Run the test suite and report PASS or FAIL."""
    r = subprocess.run(["pytest", "-q"], capture_output=True, text=True)
    return "PASS" if r.returncode == 0 else "FAIL\n" + r.stdout[-2000:]

model = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4.1-mini")
coder = AssistantAgent("coder", model_client=model,
                       system_message="Write the patch.")
reviewer = AssistantAgent("reviewer", model_client=model, tools=[run_tests],
                          system_message="Call run_tests. Say APPROVED only if it passes.")

last = {}
def repeated(msgs) -> bool:                # called with new messages only
    for m in msgs:
        if m.source == "coder":
            if last.get("coder") == m.to_text():
                return True                # same patch twice in a row
            last["coder"] = m.to_text()
    return False

stop = (TextMentionTermination("APPROVED")
        | MaxMessageTermination(30)
        | TokenUsageTermination(max_total_token=100_000)
        | TimeoutTermination(timeout_seconds=720)
        | FunctionalTermination(repeated))

team = RoundRobinGroupChat([coder, reviewer], termination_condition=stop)
result = asyncio.run(team.run(task="Fix the failing invoice-rounding test"))
print(result.stop_reason)
mafail.note: Replace the model name with a current one. Termination conditions receive only the messages since their last call, so the repetition check keeps the previous patch itself.

lib: Its Send API does map-reduce: a conditional edge returns one Send per item, each worker node receives only its own slice of state, and a reducer such as operator.add collects the results.

import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import Send

SECTOR = {"usd_inr": 86.4, "api_price_index": 112.0}      # computed once

class Research(TypedDict):
    companies: list[str]
    cards: Annotated[list[dict], operator.add]              # reducer: parallel writes append

class One(TypedDict):                                       # a worker sees only this
    company: str
    sector: dict

def analyse_company(company: str, sector: dict) -> dict:
    """Stub: call your model with the brief and this company's filings only."""
    return {"company": company, "revenue_cr": 0.0, "usd_inr_used": sector["usd_inr"],
            "red_flags": [], "sources": [f"filings/{company}/q2.pdf"]}

def fan_out(state: Research):
    return [Send("analyse", {"company": c, "sector": SECTOR}) for c in state["companies"]]

def analyse(slice_: One):
    card = analyse_company(slice_["company"], slice_["sector"])
    return {"cards": [card]}                                # a short card, not a transcript

def merge_check(state: Research):
    rates = {c["usd_inr_used"] for c in state["cards"]}
    seen = {c["company"] for c in state["cards"]}
    missing = [c for c in state["companies"] if c not in seen]
    return {"cards": [{"merge_check": {"conflicting_rates": sorted(rates) if len(rates) > 1 else [],
                                       "missing": missing}}]}

g = StateGraph(Research)
g.add_node("analyse", analyse)
g.add_node("merge_check", merge_check)
g.add_conditional_edges(START, fan_out, ["analyse"])
g.add_edge("analyse", "merge_check")
g.add_edge("merge_check", END)
app = g.compile()

names = ["Arogya", "Sanjivani", "Nilgiri", "Kaveri", "Vindhya", "Tapti",
         "Sahyadri", "Narmada", "Godavari", "Aravalli", "Konkan", "Chambal"]
out = app.invoke({"companies": names, "cards": []}, config={"max_concurrency": 6})
print(len(out["cards"]), out["cards"][-1])
subagents.note: analyse_company() is a stub for your own model call (any SDK). LangGraph runs the Send branches in the same superstep, in parallel; cap concurrency with the max_concurrency key in the run config if your model provider rate-limits you.

mafail.scenario: A SaaS firm runs 50 overnight coder–reviewer runs. A run needs 8 to 26 messages; each message costs 4k tokens and 20 seconds. Eight runs fall into a loop, re-sending the same patch; six claim APPROVED too early; and some agents simply forget to say APPROVED. Runs that nothing stops are killed by hand at 60 messages (240k tokens).
controls: Toggle message (30), token (100k, 25 messages) and time (12 minutes, 36 messages) caps.
Toggle a repetition detector and a verifier that runs the tests before APPROVED counts.
Choose AND or OR to combine the stop signal and caps, and set how often agents forget to say APPROVED.
outputs: Runs that no condition ever stops.
Including runs killed by hand, against what the work needs.
Runs ended before the work was done: false APPROVED claims or a cap reached too soon.
Looping runs stopped by a cap, returning a partial result.
Runs that ended on an APPROVED claim nobody checked.

presets.name: No stop rules
presets.expect: No caps: 15 of 50 runs never end (8 loops and 7 that never say APPROVED), 6 stop early on false claims, 35 outputs ship unchecked, and runs average 116.1k tokens (1.72× what the work needs).

presets.name: Caps combined with AND
presets.expect: All three caps, but with AND: still 15 endless runs, because AND waits for an APPROVED that never comes; the rest run on to message 36. 172.8k tokens per run (2.56×), 35 unverified.

presets.name: AND caps with a verifier
presets.expect: The verifier ends false claims and unverified outputs (0), but the 8 loops never pass their tests, so they are still endless under AND. 159.4k per run (2.36×).

presets.name: Repetition detector only
presets.expect: The detector breaks the 8 loops, but 7 runs that never say APPROVED are endless, 6 stop early and 43 outputs ship unchecked. 90.5k per run (1.34×).

missions.text: Get endless runs to 0.
missions.hint: Turn on at least one cap and combine with OR.

missions.text: With at least two caps on, keep premature stops at 2 or fewer and no endless runs.
missions.hint: False APPROVED claims and a tight token cap both stop runs too soon. The verifier catches one; the other is a cap to drop.

missions.text: With the verifier on, ship 0 unverified outputs at under 1.3× the base tokens, with no endless runs.

whenmulti.title: Estimating a multi-agent run
whenmulti.code:
branches = independent_branches(graph)
branch_min = [sum(t.minutes for t in b) for b in branches]
branch_tokens = [sum(t.tokens for t in b) for b in branches]
wall = max(branch_min) + MERGE_MIN
tokens = max(branch_tokens)
cost_inr = tokens / 1000 * INR_PER_1K
whenmulti.explain: Parallelism saves time, not tokens. Every branch still consumes its own tokens, so the bill is the sum of all branches plus the orchestrator’s own tokens. Taking the maximum makes a team look almost as cheap as one agent.

also.2: Summing within a branch is right: steps inside one branch run in order.
also.4: max is right for wall time: parallel branches finish when the slowest one does, plus the merge.

supervisor.title: Creating worker sub-agents
supervisor.code:
for task in plan.tasks:
    workers[task.id] = AgentDefinition(
        description=f"Researches {task.title}.",
        prompt=task.title,
        tools=["Read", "Grep", "WebFetch"],
        model="sonnet",
    )
supervisor.explain: A sub-agent starts with a fresh context: it sees only its own prompt and the brief it is given, not the parent conversation. A title such as “Check competitor pricing” gives it no objective, output format, sources or boundaries, so workers overlap, wander and return inconsistent results.

also.3: A short description is fine: it tells the orchestrator when to use the worker.
also.5: A read-and-fetch tool list is appropriate least privilege for a research worker.

handoffs.title: Handoffs for a bank support bot
handoffs.code:
card = handoff(card_agent,
    tool_description_override="Blocked or declined debit and credit cards.")
loan = handoff(loan_agent,
    tool_description_override="Blocked or declined debit and credit cards.")
triage = Agent(name="Triage", instructions="Route to the right specialist.",
               handoffs=[card, loan])
result = await Runner.run(triage, user_text, max_turns=8)
handoffs.explain: Handoffs are tools, and the triage model chooses among them by their descriptions. The loan handoff was copied from the card one, so both tools promise the same thing and triage has nothing to route on: EMI questions go to the card agent half the time.
handoffs.fix: tool_description_override="Loan EMIs, bounced EMIs, foreclosure and loan statements.")

also.2: A specific description for the card agent is exactly right.
also.7: max_turns=8 is a sensible cap on the whole run.

sharedstate.title: A shared board for parallel agents
sharedstate.explain: Three parallel nodes write the same key in the same step, and the key has no reducer. LangGraph cannot choose between the values and raises InvalidUpdateError; with sequential writes the list would simply be overwritten. Either way findings are lost.

also.4: decision has a single writer (the dispatcher), so replacing it is fine.
also.8: Joining the three branches before the dispatcher is correct.

debate.title: A three-agent coverage debate
debate.code:
async def debate(agents, q, rounds=2):
    answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(a, q) for a in agents))
    for _ in range(rounds):
        peers = "\n---\n".join(answers)
        answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(a, q, peers) for a in agents))
    final = label(answers[-1])
    return final
debate.explain: answers[-1] is just the last agent in the list, so the group’s work is thrown away and accuracy falls back to one agent’s. The answer should be the majority of the final round, or a judge’s decision with a rubric.
debate.fix: final = Counter(label(x) for x in answers).most_common(1)[0][0]

also.2: Independent first answers, run in parallel, are the right start.
also.4: Sharing every answer with every agent is the debate step itself.

mafail.title: Stopping a coder–reviewer team
mafail.code:
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import TextMentionTermination, MaxMessageTermination
from autogen_agentchat.teams import RoundRobinGroupChat

stop = TextMentionTermination("TERMINATE") & MaxMessageTermination(20)
team = RoundRobinGroupChat([coder, reviewer], termination_condition=stop)
result = await team.run(task="Fix the failing invoice test")
print(result.stop_reason)
mafail.explain: & means both conditions must have fired, so the run stops only after TERMINATE has been said and 20 messages have passed. If no agent ever says TERMINATE, the message cap never ends the run. Safety caps must be combined with | so that any one of them stops it.

also.5: Passing the combined condition to the team is right.
also.7: Logging stop_reason is good practice: it says which condition fired.

subagents.title: A fan-out that is not parallel
subagents.code:
async def fan_out(companies):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(6)
    cards = []
    for co in companies:
        cards.append(await analyse(co, sem))
    return cards
subagents.explain: Each await finishes before the loop starts the next company, so only one session ever runs and the semaphore never has more than one holder. Twelve 10-minute analyses take about 120 minutes instead of two waves of about 20, and one failure stops the loop and loses the cards collected so far.
subagents.fix:
return await asyncio.gather(*(analyse(co, sem) for co in companies),
                                return_exceptions=True)

also.2: A semaphore of 6 is a sensible cap; it only matters once the calls actually run together.
also.3: Collecting results in a list is fine; the problem is when each call is awaited.

2: Which tasks can run at the same time?
The five filings, because none needs another’s output
All six, including the valuation
The valuation needs all five filings, so it must wait; the filings share no inputs.
3: One filing needs about 8k tokens of working context. Does a branch fit one window?
No: split it further
Yes, easily: 8k is far below 200k
A branch only has to fit its own context window, and 8k is a small fraction of it.
4: Will five parallel agents use fewer tokens than one agent doing the same work?
No: about 150k against 40k
Yes: each reads less
Each branch still spends its own tokens, and coordination adds more. Anthropic reports about 15× chat for multi-agent against about 4× for one agent.
5: Five 6-minute reads run in parallel, then a 1-minute merge. How long does it take?
30 minutes
7 minutes
Parallel time is the slowest branch plus merging: 6 + 1 = 7.
6: 23 minutes saved at INR 20 a minute, against 110k extra tokens at INR 0.5 per 1,000. Split?
Yes: INR 460 against INR 55
No: the tokens cost more
The time is worth far more than the extra tokens here. Change either price and the answer can flip.

2: The screeners only read papers. Which tools should they get?
Read, Grep and Glob
Every tool, in case they need one
Least privilege: a reader that cannot write cannot damage shared files.
3: What does a worker know about the task when it starts?
Everything the orchestrator has seen so far
Only its own prompt and the brief it is given
A sub-agent starts with a fresh context, so the brief must carry the objective, format, sources and limits.
4: How long does the fan-out take compared with running workers one by one?
About as long as the slowest worker
The sum of all four
Workers run concurrently, so the fan-out finishes when the slowest one does.
5: Each worker read about 30k tokens. What reaches the orchestrator?
All 120k tokens of reading
About 1k per worker: its final message
Only the final message returns, so the orchestrator holds about 2k of its own plus 4k of summaries.
6: Two PDFs could not be read. What should the merged output do?
Leave them out quietly
List them as gaps for the reviewer
Synthesis includes saying what is missing, so a human knows what was not checked.

2: Why do the handoff descriptions matter?
The triage model routes on them
They are only shown in logs
Handoffs are tools, and the model picks tools by their names and descriptions.
3: After triage hands off to the card agent, who answers the user?
Triage, relaying the card agent’s reply
The card agent, directly
A handoff transfers ownership: the specialist becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn.
4: What does input_type add to the handoff?
A typed payload the model fills in when it transfers
A faster model for the specialist
The model must supply structured fields, here the last four digits and the reason, which the specialist can rely on.
5: What does the card agent see after remove_all_tools?
The conversation without earlier tool calls
Nothing at all from before the handoff
The filter trims tool calls and outputs from the history; the messages and the stored payload remain.
6: Specialists keep handing the chat back and forth. What stops it?
Nothing: it ends when the user leaves
max_turns, which raises MaxTurnsExceeded
max_turns caps the whole run, handoffs included.

2: Which field can safely use plain replacement?
findings, because it is a list
decision, because only the dispatcher writes it
Replacement is safe for a single writer. Fields written by several agents need a reducer.
3: Two nodes write findings in the same step. What does the append reducer do?
Keeps both entries
Keeps whichever arrives last
operator.add concatenates the updates, so nothing is lost.
4: Should the dispatcher read the whole board?
Yes, always read everything
No, only the findings it needs to decide
Scoped reads cut tokens and keep the agent focused.
5: The dispatcher reroutes a shipment. How can a reviewer check why?
Ask the dispatcher to explain
Follow the agent and source on each finding
Provenance on every entry makes the decision traceable to the carrier API and the IMD bulletin.
6: With typed messages instead of a board, what does each agent see?
Only messages addressed to it
Every message any agent sent
Messages go to named recipients, which scopes reads by construction.

2: What do agents see in the sharing step?
Only the majority answer
Each other’s answers and reasons
Reasons are what let an agent notice the clause it missed.
3: A3 said not covered and now reads the others’ day-care clause. What is it asked to do?
Revise or defend its answer
Copy the majority
Agents may change their answer or argue for it; a good argument can also persuade the others.
4: All three agree after round 1. What happens to round 2?
It runs anyway
It is skipped
Stopping early on agreement saves the calls a further round would cost.
5: How is the final answer chosen?
Majority of the final round
The last agent to speak
The last speaker is one agent’s view; the group’s answer is the vote or a judge’s decision.
6: Round 0 was already 2 against 1 for covered. What would plain voting have returned?
Covered, in 3 calls
Not covered
The vote already had the right answer, which is why debate must beat voting at equal cost to be worth it.

2: An agent forgets to say APPROVED. What still ends the run?
The first cap it reaches
Nothing
Caps do not depend on the agents remembering to stop.
3: Caps are combined with AND and nobody says APPROVED. When does the run stop?
At the first cap
Never
AND waits until every condition has fired, and one of them never does.
4: The coder sends the same patch twice in a row. What should happen?
Keep going: the reviewer will notice
The repetition check fires and the loop is interrupted
Step repetition is the most common MAST failure mode, so detect it rather than hope.
5: The reviewer says APPROVED but has not run the tests. Does the run stop?
Yes: APPROVED was said
Not in this design: APPROVED counts only after run_tests passes
A verifier turns a claim of done into a checked result.
6: The token cap fires first. What should the caller get?
A partial patch with the stop reason
An empty result
Partial work plus the reason lets a person pick it up instead of starting again.

2: Twelve sub-agents each look up the USD/INR rate themselves. What is the risk?
Duplicated work, and companies compared on different rates
None: every lookup returns the same rate
Each lookup costs tokens, and sub-agents that cannot see each other may pick different dates or sources. Compute the rate once and put it in every brief.
3: 12 sessions of 10 minutes each, with Semaphore(6). Roughly how long does the fan-out take?
About 20 minutes: two waves of six
About 120 minutes
Six run at a time, so the twelve go in two waves. Parallel time is the waves times the slowest session, not the sum.
4: What does the orchestrator receive from each session?
Its full transcript, about 80k tokens
Its final result, validated as a card under 500 tokens
Only the ResultMessage is used, and it must parse as a Card. The raw reading stays inside the session.
5: One session times out. With return_exceptions=True, what happens to the other eleven cards?
They are kept; the missing company is retried once and then reported
They are all lost because gather raises
The exception is returned in its slot instead of raised, so the other results survive and the gap is named.
6: 12 cards of 0.5k, 12 briefs of 0.5k and 2k of its own: how big is the orchestrator’s context?
14k tokens
960k tokens
2 + 6 + 6 = 14k. 960k is what twelve 80k transcripts would have been.
