whenmulti: A research desk must compare the quarterly results of 12 companies on results day. Each company’s filing can be read and summarised on its own. Which design fits best?
One agent reading all 12 filings in turn
One sub-agent per company, run in parallel, with an orchestrator that merges the summaries
A debate between three agents on each filing
A triage agent that hands the chat to one company specialist at a time
The filings are independent and together too large for one context, which is exactly where parallel sub-agents pay for their extra tokens.
A team plans to split a refactor of three tightly coupled modules across five coding agents. What is the main risk?
The agents will run out of tools
Each agent makes implicit design decisions that conflict with the others’
The refactor will finish too quickly to review
Parallel agents cannot use version control
Coupled work carries decisions that must agree. Cognition warns that conflicting implicit decisions produce bad results; one agent with context compression is safer here.
Eight contracts in a data room can each be reviewed independently in 5 minutes, and merging the reviews takes 2 minutes. How long does a parallel team take?
Parallel wall time is the slowest branch plus merging: 5 + 2 = 7 minutes.
A job needs about 12k chat-equivalent tokens. Using the rough multipliers of 4× for one agent and 15× for a multi-agent team, how many extra tokens does the team use?
Which signs suggest a due-diligence job is a good fit for several agents? Select all that apply.
The documents can each be reviewed without reading the others
The material is far larger than one context window
Every section edits one shared, evolving draft
Agents must agree on each intermediate decision before moving on
Independence and size favour a team. A shared evolving draft and step-by-step agreement are coupling, which favours one agent.
Four claim files can be checked in parallel, 6 minutes each, plus 1 minute to merge. What is the team’s wall time as a share of one agent doing them in turn?
An EdTech lab is reading Anthropic’s report on its research system. What share of the performance variance on BrowseComp did token usage alone explain?
Anthropic reported that token usage by itself explained 80% of the variance, which is why multi-agent gains and costs go together.
An e-commerce firm moves catalogue research from one agent to a team of five. Which of these typically rise? Select all that apply.
Wall time for work that really is parallel
Tokens, coordination and debugging effort all grow. Wall time for parallel work falls, which is the reason to split.
A bank split a credit memo into four agents, one per section. The memo came back with contradictory assumptions about the borrower’s cash flow. What is the best fix?
Add a fifth agent to vote on each section
Give each agent a larger context window
Write the memo with one agent, or share full context and traces with every writer
Run the four agents in sequence instead of in parallel
The sections are coupled. One agent, or agents that share the full context and traces, avoids conflicting implicit decisions.
One agent uses 40k tokens and takes 30 minutes; a team uses 150k tokens and takes 7 minutes. Tokens cost INR 0.5 per 1,000 and a saved minute is worth INR 2. Should you split?
No: INR 46 of time saved is less than INR 55 of extra tokens
Extra tokens: 110k × INR 0.5 per 1,000 = INR 55. Time saved: 23 × INR 2 = INR 46. The team costs more than it saves.
In the same job (INR 55 of extra tokens to save 23 minutes), at what value of a saved minute does the team break even?
Break-even is INR 55 ÷ 23 minutes ≈ INR 2.39 a minute.
A network-audit job has 6 subtasks of 5 minutes each. Four form a chain (each needs the one before) and two are independent. Merging takes 1 minute. How long does a parallel team take?
The chain of 4 runs in order: 4 × 5 = 20 minutes, plus 1 to merge = 21. The two independent subtasks finish alongside it.
When is one agent the better choice? Select all that apply.
A discharge summary where every section depends on the same patient notes
A small job that nobody is waiting for
Reading material ten times the size of one context window
Coupled work and small, unhurried jobs suit one agent. Many independent sources or material far beyond one window favour a team.
Each of 8 carrier investigations needs about 60k tokens of working context; a window holds 200k. Why might a team be justified here even at a higher token bill?
Each investigation fits one window, but all eight (480k) do not fit in one agent’s context
Sub-agents use fewer tokens per investigation
A team avoids any need to merge results
Coverage is the other reason to split: the whole job overflows one context, while each branch fits.
A payments team wants Claude sub-agents with isolated contexts and a hard spend cap for each query. Which tool feature fits?
Claude Agent SDK sub-agents with max_budget_usd
The Claude Agent SDK defines sub-agents with their own context and tools, and max_budget_usd caps the whole query, sub-agents included.
An airline’s engineering manager reads Cognition’s “Don’t build multi-agents”. What does the post recommend for long tasks?
Many parallel agents that never share context
One single-threaded agent that shares full context, with context compression for long tasks
A debate among three agents per step
A new agent for every tool call
The post argues for sharing context and full traces, and recommends a single-threaded agent with compression over parallel agents with partial context.
Before deciding between one agent and a team, which numbers do you need? Select all that apply.
How many branches share no inputs
What a saved minute is worth against the price of tokens
How many tools are in your tool registry
The decision rests on parallel branches and on the value of time versus tokens. Parameter counts and registry size do not decide it.
Ten independent subtasks need 3k chat-equivalent tokens each. A team uses about 15× that. At USD 3 per million tokens, what does the team’s run cost?
A coding-assistant start-up wants to copy Anthropic’s parallel research design for bug fixing. What does Anthropic’s post say about coding?
It is the best fit for multi-agent systems
It is a poorer fit, because it has fewer truly parallel pieces and more shared context
The post notes that domains needing shared context, such as most coding, have fewer parallelisable tasks.
You are deciding whether a contract-review job should use several agents. Which steps belong in the decision? Select all that apply.
Draw the task graph with each step’s inputs
Check that each branch fits one context window
Estimate tokens and wall time for both designs
Start with as many agents as the API allows, then trim
Graph, context check and cost estimate come first. Starting with the maximum number of agents burns tokens before you know you need them.
supervisor: Four pharmacovigilance workers keep reading the same papers and returning overlapping findings. What is the most likely cause?
The workers use a small model
Their briefs lack clear boundaries: which drugs and sources each one owns
They return summaries instead of transcripts
Without task boundaries each worker guesses its scope, so they overlap. A complete brief gives each one its own slice.
An orchestrator uses 3k tokens of its own and starts 5 workers. Each returns a 1.2k summary. How many tokens does the orchestrator hold after collecting them?
A compliance orchestrator briefs a sanctions-screening worker. What must the brief contain? Select all that apply.
The objective and the output format
The sources to use and where the task ends
The orchestrator’s full conversation so far
A worker needs its objective, format, sources and boundaries. Passing the whole parent conversation or other workers’ prompts adds tokens without helping it.
In the Claude Agent SDK, what does a (non-fork) sub-agent receive from its parent?
Only the Agent tool’s prompt string, plus its own system prompt and tools
The parent’s system prompt and tool results
Nothing until it asks for context
The only content passed from parent to sub-agent is the Agent tool’s prompt, so it must carry whatever the sub-agent needs.
Four workers each read about 30k tokens. The orchestrator uses 2k of its own. If workers return 1k summaries instead of full transcripts, how many tokens stay out of the orchestrator’s context?
A code-review orchestrator starts style, security and test-coverage workers. None of them should change files. Which tool list fits the reviewers?
All tools, since they may need one
Least privilege: reviewers need to read and search, not edit or run commands.
A shopping assistant’s orchestrator started 50 workers for “Which phone has the best camera under INR 30,000?”. What likely allowed this? Select all that apply.
No guidance on how much effort a query deserves
No cap on concurrency or spend
A vague objective in the orchestrator’s instructions
Anthropic saw early orchestrators spawn 50 sub-agents for simple queries. Effort guidance, clear objectives and caps prevent it; summaries are not the cause.
With the Claude Agent SDK defaults, how many sub-agents can run at once before new spawns are refused?
The default concurrency limit is 20; it can be lowered with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS.
A LangGraph team is choosing how to build a supervisor. What does LangChain currently recommend?
The langgraph-supervisor library for all new projects
Building the supervisor directly with tool calling
A swarm of peer agents instead
LangChain’s reference notes that it now recommends supervisors built with tool calling rather than the langgraph-supervisor library.
Six workers each read 40k tokens at about 10k tokens a minute, then the orchestrator merges for 1 minute. What is the wall time?
Each worker takes 40k ÷ 10k = 4 minutes in parallel, plus 1 minute to merge = 5 minutes.
How does a supervisor differ from a fixed execution graph? Select all that apply.
A supervisor decides how to split the task at run time
A graph fixes its steps in advance
A supervisor cannot run workers in parallel
A graph cannot call language models
The difference is who decides the steps and when. Both can run work in parallel and both can call models.
Where should the human safety reviewer sit in a pharmacovigilance screen run by an orchestrator and workers?
Before each worker starts, approving its brief
After synthesis, checking the merged findings and listed gaps
Nowhere: the orchestrator is the check
Inside every worker, reading each paper
Reviewing the merged findings, including what could not be read, puts human judgement where it adds most at the lowest cost.
A legal research team has four reading workers and one that files the final memo into the matter folder. How should write access be granted?
Only to the filing worker, and only for its output location
To none; the orchestrator writes instead of the filing worker
Least privilege per agent: only the worker that must write gets write access, scoped to where it writes.
A research query with Claude sub-agents reaches its max_budget_usd. What happens?
The SDK silently raises the budget
New sub-agents are refused and the query ends with a budget error result
Only the orchestrator stops; workers carry on
At the cap the SDK refuses further sub-agents, stops background ones and ends the query with the error_max_budget_usd subtype.
A network-operations orchestrator struggles to merge its workers’ results. Which output rules help? Select all that apply.
A fixed JSON schema for every worker’s return
A length limit on each return
Free-form prose so nothing is lost
The full transcript attached to every return
A fixed, compact format makes results comparable and keeps the orchestrator’s context small. Prose and transcripts make merging harder.
Four workers read 240k tokens in total, and 25% of that reading is duplicated because their scopes overlap. How many tokens are wasted?
25% of 240k = 60k tokens spent reading what another worker already read.
A team studies Magentic-One’s orchestrator. What does it keep to plan and track progress?
A task ledger and a progress ledger
A single system prompt with no state
Magentic-One’s orchestrator maintains a task ledger (facts, guesses, plan) and a progress ledger, and replans when progress stalls.
Claims arrive with different mixes of documents, so the subtasks are not known until the claim is read. Which Anthropic pattern fits?
Orchestrator–workers, where a central model breaks down the task and delegates at run time
Parallelization with a fixed set of sections
Anthropic describes orchestrator–workers as a central LLM that dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them and synthesizes results.
You are designing a supervisor for a hospital’s research team. Which choices apply least privilege and bounded growth? Select all that apply.
Only the report worker can write, to the report folder
Every worker gets shell access in case it needs to install tools
Read-only readers, one scoped writer and a depth cap keep the team safe and bounded. Blanket shell access is the opposite of least privilege.
A logistics team sets CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to 1. What changes?
Only one sub-agent can run at a time
Sub-agents cannot spawn sub-agents of their own
The orchestrator cannot spawn any sub-agents
Each sub-agent may use only one tool
Depth 1 stops sub-agents from spawning further layers; concurrency is a separate limit.
handoffs: A bank’s triage agent keeps sending EMI questions to the card agent. The card and loan handoffs have almost identical descriptions. What is the fix?
Distinct descriptions that say exactly when to transfer to each specialist
Passing the full history on every handoff
Handoffs are tools, and the model routes on their descriptions. Overlapping descriptions leave it guessing.
In the OpenAI Agents SDK, what is the default tool name for a handoff to an agent named “Refund agent”?
Handoffs appear to the model as tools named transfer_to_<agent_name> by default.
When should a telecom support bot use a handoff rather than calling a specialist as a tool? Select all that apply.
The specialist should talk to the user directly for the rest of the chat
The specialist has its own permissions and should own the case
A manager must combine three specialists’ answers into one reply
The manager needs a one-off sub-answer inside its own reply
A handoff transfers ownership. When one agent should keep control and compose the reply, call specialists as tools.
Of 2,000 transferred chats, 30% make the user repeat their details, adding 3 turns each at about 1.2k tokens a turn. How many tokens do the repeats cost?
An airline’s rebooking and baggage agents hand a chat back and forth until the run passes max_turns. What does the OpenAI Agents SDK do?
Hands the chat to a human automatically
Exceeding max_turns raises MaxTurnsExceeded, which you can catch to escalate.
What is input_filter for on a handoff?
Choosing which agent receives the handoff
Controlling which parts of the conversation history the receiving agent sees
An input filter transforms the history passed on, for example removing earlier tool calls.
An insurer’s claims bot bounces chats between its policy and claims agents. What can cause this? Select all that apply.
A typed payload on each handoff
Ping-pong comes from ambiguous ownership and missing limits. A typed payload helps the receiver; it does not cause bouncing.
In LangGraph, what does a handoff tool return to move control to another agent in the parent graph?
A plain string naming the agent
LangGraph handoff tools return a Command that names the next node, updates state and targets the parent graph.
A bank’s triage routes 500 chats with 88% accuracy. Each misroute costs 2 extra handoffs before the chat lands. How many extra handoffs is that?
An airline wants the triage model to supply the PNR and the reason when it hands off to the refunds agent. Which feature fits?
input_type makes the model fill in a structured payload when it calls the handoff.
A hospital’s intake agent hands patients to a scheduling agent. What should travel with the handoff? Select all that apply.
A typed payload with the facts scheduling needs
The conversation with earlier tool calls filtered out
Every internal tool call and raw tool output
Nothing, so the specialist starts unbiased
Pass the needed facts and a trimmed history. Raw tool output wastes tokens; nothing at all makes the patient repeat themselves.
A travel assistant built with langgraph-swarm resumes a returning user’s chat. Which agent answers first?
The agent recorded in the active_agent state key
The agent with the shortest description
langgraph-swarm tracks active_agent so a conversation resumes with whichever agent last owned it.
A student-support triage agent hands a fee query to the fees agent. Who replies to the student next?
The triage agent, relaying the fees agent’s answer
Both agents, one after the other
No one until a human approves
After a handoff the specialist becomes the active agent and answers directly.
How does a handoff differ from model routing?
Routing picks a model for one request; a handoff moves ownership of the conversation, with its state, to another agent
A handoff always uses a smaller model
Routing needs several agents; handoffs need one
Routing is a per-request model choice. A handoff changes which agent owns the rest of the conversation.
Passing the full history adds 14 messages of about 0.4k tokens to each handoff, and chats average 1.4 handoffs. How many extra tokens per chat is that?
What is the on_handoff callback useful for? Select all that apply.
Logging or fetching data at the moment of the handoff
Storing the typed payload where the specialist can read it
Choosing which agent the handoff goes to
on_handoff runs when the handoff happens, so it can log, fetch data or store the payload. The model chooses the target; max_turns is a run setting.
An AutoGen support team must pause when an agent needs the customer to supply an OTP. Which termination condition fits?
HandoffTermination stops the team when an agent hands off to the named target, here the user.
The fraud agent can freeze cards; the triage agent cannot. Why keep permissions per specialist?
Each agent gets only the privileges its job needs, so a misrouted or manipulated agent can do less harm
Per-agent permissions apply least privilege: the tools that can change things sit only with the agent that owns that job.
Which make good handoff descriptions for a telecom bot’s specialists? Select all that apply.
Naming topics that are distinct for each specialist
Using one generic sentence for all of them, for consistency
Specific, distinct, non-overlapping descriptions give the triage model something to route on. A shared generic sentence removes that.
On 20 test chats, triage routes 17 correctly. How many more must it get right to reach the 90% target?
90% of 20 is 18, so it needs one more correct route.
sharedstate: Three parallel LangGraph nodes each return {"findings": [x]} into a key declared as findings: list[str]. What happens?
LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError, because the key has no reducer and receives several values in one step
Only the first write is kept
Without a reducer LangGraph cannot choose between concurrent values for one key, so it rejects the update.
How do you fix that board so all three findings are kept?
Run the nodes one after another
Rename the key in each node
operator.add is a reducer that concatenates the updates, so parallel writes merge.
A claim file is shared by several agents. Which fields need a reducer? Select all that apply.
Findings written by the document, fraud and coverage agents
Open questions that any agent may add
The final decision, written only by the adjudicator
The claim ID, set once at the start
Fields with several writers need a merge rule. Single-writer or write-once fields can use plain replacement.
Five agents each write 6 findings of about 0.5k tokens, and every agent then reads the whole board. How many tokens do the five agents read in total?
The board holds 5 × 6 × 0.5k = 15k tokens; five agents each read it: 5 × 15k = 75k.
On the same board, each agent reads only the findings of the 2 writers it depends on. How many tokens do the five agents read in total?
An AML team asks every agent to record its name and source on each finding. What does this buy?
An audit trail: every statement in the note can be traced to who wrote it and where it came from
Provenance makes findings auditable, which regulators and analysts need.
Agents coordinate through a free-text group chat. What problems are likely? Select all that apply.
Findings are buried in prose and missed
Parallel writes are rejected with an error
Free text keeps every message but buries findings, loses sources and makes everyone read everything. Rejected writes are a typed-state problem.
A bank’s KYC agent must discover what a vendor’s document-verification agent can do before sending it work over A2A. What does it read?
In A2A, an Agent Card advertises an agent’s identity, capabilities and how to reach it.
In MetaGPT, how do role agents share work?
Each role reads every chat message
Roles publish structured documents to a shared message pool and subscribe to what their role needs
Roles hand off the conversation one by one
MetaGPT uses a shared message pool with publish–subscribe by role, which scopes what each agent reads.
A board replaces the findings list on every write. Three parallel writers produce 6, 4 and 5 findings, and the writer with 5 finishes last. How many findings are lost?
Only the last write survives: 5 of 15 kept, so 10 are lost.
When is typed message passing a better fit than a shared board? Select all that apply.
The agents belong to different organisations or systems
You need a record of who sent what to whom
All agents live in one graph and feed one decision
Only one agent does all the work
Messages suit separate systems and auditable exchanges. One graph feeding one decision is the board’s home ground; one agent needs neither.
In LangGraph, a node updates a key that has no reducer, and no other node writes it in that step. What happens to the old value?
It is kept and the update ignored
The default for a key without a reducer is to overwrite it with the new value.
A chat app’s LangGraph state uses add_messages for its messages key. What does that reducer do?
Merges new messages into the list, updating any with the same ID
add_messages appends new messages and updates existing ones that share an ID.
A claim file has 60 entries, and 48 of them name both the agent and the source. What is the provenance rate?
What did the 2025 blackboard multi-agent paper (Han et al.) report against static and dynamic multi-agent baselines?
The best average performance while spending fewer tokens
Higher accuracy at triple the tokens
The authors report the best average performance across their datasets with fewer tokens than the baselines.
A research team’s board holds prices, news, filings and analyst notes. Which read rules scope reads well? Select all that apply.
The valuation agent reads only prices and filings
Each agent reads only the fields it needs
Every agent reads the full board to be safe
Writers re-read their own output on every step
Scoped reads cut tokens and distraction. Reading everything, or re-reading one’s own output, wastes context.
What role does Magentic-One’s task ledger play?
It is a shared record of facts, guesses and the plan that the orchestrator keeps up to date
The task ledger is an explicit shared record that the orchestrator uses to plan and replan.
The carrier agent reports an ETA of Friday; the warehouse agent reports Saturday. How should the board handle it?
Keep both, each with its agent, source and time, and resolve them by a stated rule or escalate
With provenance on both entries, a rule (for example, trust the carrier’s scan data) or a person can resolve the conflict transparently.
An incident board records findings from log, metrics and deploy agents. Which fields should each entry carry? Select all that apply.
Author, source and time make entries traceable and orderable. The system prompt adds tokens without helping anyone audit the finding.
A board holds 40 findings of 0.8k tokens. The dispatcher’s read scope covers 25% of them. How many tokens does it read?
debate: Three independent agents are each right 80% of the time. What is the accuracy of their majority vote?
Four agents answer, then debate for 2 rounds, and a judge decides. How many model calls is that?
When is debate most likely to help a health insurer’s coverage checks? Select all that apply.
The agents’ errors are fairly independent
The answer rests on a clause others can check
All agents use the same model and the same prompt
A human assessor already reviews every case
Independent errors and checkable arguments let agents correct each other. Identical agents share blind spots, and a full human review makes the extra calls redundant.
Which setup did Du et al. (2023) mainly use for their multiagent-debate results?
Their main experiments used 3 agents and 2 rounds, for example lifting GSM8K from 77.0% to 85.0%.
What did Choi, Zhu and Li (NeurIPS 2025) find about multi-agent debate across seven benchmarks?
Majority voting alone accounts for most of the gains attributed to debate
They found voting explains most of debate’s gains, so compare against voting before paying for rounds.
A debate function ends with final = answers[-1]. What is wrong?
Nothing: the last answer is the most refined
It takes the last agent’s answer instead of the group’s majority
The last speaker is one agent. The final answer should be a majority vote of the final round or a judge’s decision.
What can go wrong in multi-agent debate? Select all that apply.
Agents conform to a confident but wrong peer
An agent sticks to its first answer (degeneration of thought)
Agents with correlated errors agree on the same mistake
Conformity, anchoring and correlated errors are known failure modes. With 3 agents and two answers, a tie is impossible.

Agents are each 70% accurate. On 50% of cases they share one blind spot (all right or all wrong together); on the rest they are independent, where a 3-agent vote reaches 78.4%. What is the overall accuracy?
Liang et al. (2023) add a judge to multi-agent debate. What caution do they raise?
An LLM judge may not be fair when the debating agents use different LLMs
They warn that a judge may favour answers from its own kind of model.
Three agents debate for 3 rounds in total (the first answers plus 2 more rounds) at about 2k tokens per call. Plain voting uses only the first round. How many extra tokens does debate cost?
A diagnosis-support team wants to use disagreement between agents well. Which practices help? Select all that apply.
Send cases that stay split to a clinician
Stop early when all agents agree
Always run the maximum number of rounds
Drop the dissenting agent’s answer without reading it
Disagreement is a signal for escalation, and agreement is a reason to stop. Always maxing rounds wastes calls; ignoring dissent throws away the check.
What did Smit et al. (2023) conclude about multi-agent debate?
It reliably beats every other method
It does not reliably beat self-consistency and is more sensitive to hyperparameters
It only works with one agent
They found debate does not reliably outperform self-consistency and depends heavily on settings.
Five independent agents are each right 60% of the time. What is the majority-vote accuracy?
Four agents split 2 against 2 on whether a transaction breaches a limit. What is a sound way to settle it?
A judge with a clear rubric, or escalation to a person
Even numbers can tie. A rubric-based judge or a human settles ties transparently.
Before adding debate rounds to product-question answering, which cheaper options should you try? Select all that apply.
A majority vote over independent answers
Self-consistency: sampling one model several times and voting
Adding debate rounds to every query by default
More rounds with the same prompt and model
Voting and self-consistency capture much of the gain for fewer calls. Default or extra rounds are the costly option being tested.
Plain voting reaches 78% accuracy in 3 calls; debate reaches 80% in 9 calls. How many extra calls does each extra percentage point cost?
6 extra calls ÷ 2 extra points = 3 calls per point.
What early-stopping rule suits a debate loop?
Stop as soon as all agents give the same answer
Never stop before the maximum rounds
Stop when one agent is confident
Unanimous agreement means another round is unlikely to change the vote, so stopping saves calls.
Why is an odd number of agents often used for a majority vote?
With two possible answers, an odd number cannot tie
For a yes/no answer, an odd count guarantees a majority.
A research team wants its analyst agents’ errors to be more independent. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
Use different models for different agents
Give agents different prompts or perspectives
Give each agent a different subset of the evidence
Repeat the same temperature-0 prompt on the same model
Diversity of model, prompt and evidence reduces shared blind spots. Identical deterministic calls give identical answers.
What is “degeneration of thought” in multi-agent debate?
An agent becoming stuck on its first answer even when it is wrong, so further reflection adds nothing
Liang et al. name this problem and use debate between agents to break it.
mafail: A team uses TextMentionTermination("TERMINATE") & MaxMessageTermination(20). Neither agent ever says TERMINATE. What happens?
It never stops on its own, because & needs both conditions
It stops at the first message
It raises an error at once
& waits for both conditions; without TERMINATE it never fires. Use | so either one stops the run.
Each message uses about 4k tokens. Caps of 30 messages and 100k tokens are combined with OR. After how many messages does the run stop, if nothing else stops it?
The token cap is reached at 100k ÷ 4k = 25 messages, before the message cap.
Which are categories in the MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failures? Select all that apply.
MAST’s three categories are system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. Hardware and security issues are outside it.
According to MAST, which single failure mode is most common?
Step repetition is the most common at about 15.7%, ahead of reasoning–action mismatch (13.2%) and unawareness of stopping conditions (12.4%).
A coder–reviewer loop runs for 180 messages of about 5k tokens each. At USD 10 per million tokens, what does it cost?
A Claude Agent SDK research run reaches max_budget_usd. What happens?
It keeps going and bills later
New sub-agents are refused and the query ends with an error_max_budget_usd result
The SDK enforces the cap: it refuses new sub-agents, stops background ones and ends the query.
A bank’s overnight reconciliation team needs stop rules. Which belong in the design? Select all that apply.
An explicit stop signal that agents are told when to use
Caps on messages, tokens and time, combined with OR
A verifier that checks the result before it counts as done
Caps combined with AND so every limit is respected
A stop signal, OR-combined caps and a verifier bound the run and make done mean checked. AND lets a run continue until every condition has fired.
A LangGraph agent loop exceeds its recursion limit. What happens?
The graph silently stops and returns the last state
The limit resets and the loop continues
The graph switches to a smaller model
Reaching the recursion limit raises GraphRecursionError, which you can catch and handle.
Which OpenAI Agents SDK setting bounds the whole agent loop, including handoffs?
max_turns caps the loop; passing it raises MaxTurnsExceeded.
Messages take about 20 seconds each. A TimeoutTermination of 12 minutes corresponds to about how many messages?
You write a custom repetition check as an AutoGen FunctionalTermination. What must it do? Select all that apply.
Compare each agent’s new message with that agent’s previous one
Keep its own record of earlier messages, because it receives only new ones
Delete earlier messages from the chat
Termination conditions see only messages since their last call, so a repetition check keeps its own state and compares.
After adding a 20-message cap, 12% of legitimate refactor runs are cut off before finishing. What is the best response?
Set the cap from the distribution of successful runs, for example just above the longest normal run, and return partial work when it fires
Caps should bound failures, not normal work. Size them from real run lengths and return partial results with a reason.
A reviewer agent approves patches without running the tests, and broken code ships. Which MAST category is this?
None; it is a model bug
Skipping or weakening checks is a task-verification failure. Require a verifier, such as the test suite, before approval counts.
Of 50 runs, 8 never stop and are killed at 240k tokens; the other 42 average 70k. What is the average tokens per run?
A cap fires before a catalogue-cleanup team finishes. What should the caller receive? Select all that apply.
The partial result produced so far
The stop reason, such as which cap fired
The reviewer’s last APPROVED message, presented as final
An empty result, so no partial data is exposed
Partial work plus the reason lets a person continue. Presenting an unchecked message as final, or returning nothing, hides the failure.
Which AutoGen condition stops a team when prompt or completion tokens pass a limit?
TokenUsageTermination watches token usage; MaxMessageTermination counts messages.
The MAST study reports κ = 0.88 for its annotations. What does that number measure?
Agreement between human annotators labelling the failures
Cohen’s kappa measures inter-annotator agreement; 0.88 is strong agreement on the taxonomy.
A team combines “says DONE” AND MaxMessageTermination(30). An agent says DONE at message 12. When does the run stop?
At message 30, when both conditions have fired
With AND, each condition must have fired; DONE fired at 12 and the message cap fires at 30, so the run wastes 18 messages.
Which controls act on the team as a whole rather than on one agent’s prompt? Select all that apply.
A cap on sub-agent nesting depth
A spend cap for the whole run
Depth, concurrency and team-wide spend caps bound the team. Prompt length is a single-agent control.
Adding up MAST’s per-mode shares, which category accounts for the largest share of failures?
System design issues, such as step repetition and unawareness of stopping conditions, add up to about 44%.

Equity research
Dalal Lens Research, a fictional equity-research firm, runs 12 sub-agents, one per company, and each reads about 40k tokens of filings. What should each sub-agent send back to the orchestrator?
Its full transcript, so nothing is lost
A condensed card of at most about 500 tokens in a fixed schema, with sources
Nothing: it should write straight into the final report
The raw PDFs it read, so the orchestrator can check them
The raw reading should stay inside each isolated context. Twelve cards cost about 6k tokens in the orchestrator; twelve transcripts would be about 480k tokens of filings alone.

Banking
An orchestrator uses 2k tokens of its own plus 0.5k per brief. It fans out 16 sub-agents, and each returns a 0.5k card. How large is the orchestrator’s context after fan-in?
10k tokens
18k tokens
26k tokens
16k tokens
2k own + 16 × 0.5k of briefs + 16 × 0.5k of cards = 2 + 8 + 8 = 18k tokens.

An insurer fans out 30 independent claim reviews with a concurrency cap of 10. Each review takes 6 minutes, planning takes 1 minute and merging 2 minutes. What is the wall-clock time?
21 minutes
180 minutes
9 minutes
183 minutes
Thirty reviews at 10 at a time run in 3 waves of 6 minutes: 18 minutes. Add 1 for planning and 2 for merging: 21 minutes. Run one by one they would take 1 + 180 + 2 = 183 minutes.

Payments
A payments company plans to fan out dispute analysis across many sub-agents. Which are real costs of that design? (Select all that apply.)
More total tokens, because every sub-agent pays its own prompt, tools and reasoning
Coordination work: concurrency caps, retries and partial failures
Conflicting results when the pieces secretly share an input
A longer wall-clock than doing the disputes one by one
Fan-out saves wall-clock time, so the last option is wrong. It does cost tokens, coordination and the risk of conflicting findings when pieces are not truly independent.

Healthcare
A clinical support agent must adjust one patient’s medication plan, where every dose change affects the others. A developer proposes one parallel sub-agent per drug. What is the better design?
Keep it with one agent, because the decisions are tightly coupled
Twelve sub-agents, one per drug, to finish faster
Sub-agents that return transcripts so the orchestrator sees everything
Sub-agents with a higher temperature for more variety
Parallel sub-agents fit independent pieces. Coupled decisions split across isolated contexts produce conflicting implicit choices, so one agent with full context is safer and cheaper.

E-commerce
An e-commerce team’s fan-out code reads: for sku in skus: results.append(await check(sku)). Fifty checks of 1 minute each take 50 minutes. Why?
The semaphore is too small
Each await finishes before the next check starts, so the checks run one at a time
The model is rate-limited to one call a minute
The results list is shared between sub-agents
Awaiting inside the loop makes the fan-out sequential. Start all checks together with asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup, under a concurrency cap.

A telecom operator fans out 12 regional churn analyses. Each sub-agent estimates the national churn baseline itself, and the regional reports disagree. What is the best fix?
Add a debate round between the 12 sub-agents
Compute the baseline once in the orchestrator and pass it in every brief
Return full transcripts so the orchestrator can spot the difference
Use a larger model for each sub-agent
The regions were not independent: they shared a hidden input. Computing it once removes both the duplicated work and the source of the conflict; a merge check can then confirm everyone used it.

Udaan Lend, a fictional NBFC, fans out loan-file reviews to sub-agents. What belongs in each sub-agent’s condensed card? (Select all that apply.)
A fixed schema of the key fields, such as income, obligations and red flags
The document ids behind each claim
The shared figures and units it used, such as the policy rate and ₹ lakh

Insurance
Three sub-agents under a Google ADK ParallelAgent all save their results to the same session-state key, and only one result survives. What is the fix?
Ask the sub-agents to write shorter results
Give each sub-agent its own output_key and merge the keys afterwards
Increase the model’s context window
Ask the sub-agents to agree on one answer

Twelve company sessions are started with asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True), and one times out. What does the orchestrator get back?
Nothing: gather raises and all results are lost
Eleven results plus the exception object in the failed company’s slot
Twelve results, with the timed-out one filled in by the model
Only the results that finished before the timeout
With return_exceptions=True, exceptions are returned in place instead of raised, so the other eleven cards survive and the missing company can be retried and reported.

A law firm’s data room holds 200 contracts of about 6k tokens each. Each sub-agent has a 200k window and needs 40k for its own prompt, tools and notes. What is the smallest number of sub-agents that lets every contract be read in full?
Each sub-agent has 200k − 40k = 160k for contracts, which is 26 whole contracts of 6k. 200 ÷ 26 ≈ 7.7, so 8 sub-agents are needed.

About 1.5×

The number of sub-agents
The length of the system prompt
The sampling temperature

A bank runs KYC refresh checks for thousands of customers with fan-out. Which practices keep this safe at scale? (Select all that apply.)
A concurrency cap, such as a semaphore sized to the provider’s rate limits
A turn or budget cap on every session
Retrying failed pieces once, then reporting what is still missing
Letting every sub-agent start more sub-agents without a limit
Caps on concurrency and per-session spend, plus explicit handling of failures, keep a large fan-out predictable. Unbounded nested spawning multiplies cost and failure modes.

One agent analyses 10 regions at 9 minutes each, then merges for 2 minutes. Ten parallel sub-agents each take 9 minutes after a 3-minute start-up, then the merge takes 2 minutes. How many minutes does the parallel design save?

When is parallel fan-out a poor fit? (Select all that apply.)
The pieces are tightly coupled, so each change affects the others
The whole job fits comfortably in one context and nobody is waiting on the minutes
The pieces are independent and together overflow one window
Each piece needs the finished results of the others before it can start
Fan-out pays when pieces are independent and too big for one context. Coupled or sequential pieces, or small jobs, are cheaper and more coherent with one agent.

Two sub-agents in a UPI dispute review both analysed the same 400 transactions, because one was briefed on “March disputes” and the other on “high-value disputes”. What prevents this?
Briefs that partition the work on one key, such as non-overlapping date ranges, plus a merge check that removes duplicates by transaction id
A larger context window for each sub-agent
Returning transcripts so the orchestrator can compare them
A higher concurrency cap
Overlapping scopes cause duplicated work. Partition the pieces on a single key so they cannot overlap, and deduplicate by id at fan-in in case they still do.
