A hospital’s orchestrator uses 4k tokens of its own. Eight sub-agents would each return a 90k transcript, or a 1k card instead. How many tokens does condensing save in the orchestrator’s context?
8k
Transcripts: 4 + 8 × 90 = 724k. Cards: 4 + 8 × 1 = 12k. Saved: 724 − 12 = 712k tokens.

whenmulti.q: In your own words: when is a multi-agent system worth its extra tokens, and when is one agent better?
whenmulti.model: A team is worth it when the job splits into independent pieces that can run in parallel and together would overflow one context, such as reading many filings at once. It buys wall time and coverage, but at roughly 15× the tokens of chat against about 4× for one agent. When the work is coupled, as in coding or one valuation model, split agents make conflicting implicit decisions, so a single agent with good context management is cheaper and more coherent.

whenmulti.q: A colleague says five parallel agents will cut the bill because each reads less. What do you tell them?
whenmulti.model: Parallel agents finish sooner, but they do not use fewer tokens: every branch still reads and reasons over its share, and the orchestrator adds briefing and merging on top. Anthropic reports multi-agent systems using about 15× the tokens of chat. Estimate or measure both designs on a sample of real jobs, and split only if the time or coverage gained is worth more than the extra spend.

whenmulti.q: How would you decide, before building anything, whether a new job should use one agent or several?
pts: compare time value with token cost
whenmulti.model: Write the job as a task graph with the inputs each step needs, count the branches that share no inputs, and check that each branch fits one context window. Then estimate tokens (about 4× chat for one agent, about 15× for a team) and wall time (the slowest branch plus merging) and price both, including what a saved minute is worth. Split only if the team comes out ahead; otherwise keep one agent.

supervisor.q: What must a worker’s brief contain, and why can’t the worker simply work it out?
supervisor.model: A worker starts with a fresh context: it sees its own system prompt and the brief it is given, not the orchestrator’s conversation. So the brief must say what to find, in what format, from which sources and tools, and where its task ends. Anthropic found that vague briefs led workers to duplicate each other or misread the task.

supervisor.q: Why should workers return short summaries rather than their full transcripts?
pts: raw reading stays with the worker
supervisor.model: The point of isolation is that the raw reading stays with the worker. If every worker returns its transcript, the orchestrator’s context fills with tens of thousands of tokens it does not need, which costs more and makes the merge worse. A fixed, compact output format keeps each return to about a thousand tokens and makes the results easy to combine.

supervisor.q: Design the tool permissions for a team of research workers and one worker that files a report.
pts: only the filing worker can write
supervisor.model: Give the research workers only read and search tools, such as Read, Grep and a web fetch, so they cannot change anything. Give write access only to the single worker that files the report, and only for its output location. That is least privilege applied per agent. Add a spend cap and limits on sub-agent depth and concurrency so the orchestrator cannot spawn an unbounded tree of workers.

handoffs.q: In your own words: how is a handoff different from calling a specialist agent as a tool?
pts: as a tool, the manager keeps control
choose by who should own the reply
handoffs.model: With a handoff the triage agent gives the conversation away: the specialist becomes the active agent and answers the user directly for the rest of the turn. With an agent called as a tool, the manager keeps control, gets the specialist’s answer back and writes the reply itself. Use a handoff when the specialist should own the conversation; use agents as tools when one agent should stay in charge.

handoffs.q: Users complain they have to repeat their details after being transferred. How would you fix it without sending the whole history?
pts: store it where the specialist can read it
handoffs.model: Give the handoff a typed payload with input_type, so the triage model must fill in the facts the specialist needs, such as the mobile number, circle and issue. Store it where the specialist’s instructions can read it, and use an input filter to trim tool calls from the history. Then track how often users are asked to repeat themselves to confirm the fix.

handoffs.q: Two specialists keep transferring a chat back and forth. What would you check and change?
handoffs.model: Ping-pong usually means the handoff descriptions overlap, so each specialist thinks the other owns the case. Make the descriptions distinct and specific, cap the run with max_turns and a limit on hops, and escalate to a person when the cap is reached. Trace every handoff so you can see which pairs of agents bounce most.

sharedstate.q: In your own words: what goes wrong when several agents write to one shared state, and how do you prevent it?
sharedstate.model: When agents write the same field at once, one write can overwrite another, or in LangGraph the update is rejected because the key has no reducer. Give every multi-writer field a reducer such as operator.add so updates are merged, type the fields so findings are structured, and record the agent and source on each entry so conflicts can be traced and resolved.

sharedstate.q: When would you choose typed message passing over a shared board?
pts: each agent sees only its messages
audit trail of who told whom
sharedstate.model: A shared board suits agents inside one application that all contribute to one decision. Typed messages suit agents in separate systems or teams, where each should see only what is addressed to it and you want a record of who sent what to whom. A2A standardises such messages across vendors with Agent Cards, Tasks, Messages, Parts and Artifacts.

sharedstate.q: Every agent reads the whole board and token use is climbing. What would you change?
sharedstate.model: Scope each agent’s reads to the fields it needs, so the dispatcher reads findings and not every raw note. Compact older entries into summaries, and consider publish–subscribe by role, as MetaGPT does, so agents receive only relevant documents. Measure tokens read per agent before and after to confirm the saving.

debate.q: In your own words: when is multi-agent debate worth its cost?
debate.model: Debate multiplies calls, agents times rounds plus any judge, so it must earn that cost. It helps most when agents make fairly independent errors, the answer has a checkable argument, and mistakes are expensive. Always compare it with plain majority voting at the same cost: recent work finds voting accounts for most of debate’s gains.

debate.q: Three agents all use the same model and prompt. Why might the ensemble barely help, and what would you change?
debate.model: If the agents share a model and a prompt, they tend to make the same mistakes, so they agree confidently on a wrong answer and the vote adds little. Vary the models, prompts or evidence each agent sees to make errors more independent, and treat disagreement as a signal to escalate to a human assessor rather than forcing consensus.

debate.q: Design a coverage-check ensemble for health claims that stays within a fixed cost per claim.
debate.model: Ask three agents independently and take the majority vote. Run a debate round only when they disagree, and stop as soon as they agree, which keeps most claims at three calls. Send any case still split after that round to a human assessor, and check on labelled claims that the round actually beats voting before keeping it.

mafail.q: In your own words: why do multi-agent teams need hard caps even when agents are told when to stop?
pts: agents forget or miss the stop condition
caps do not depend on agents
mafail.model: Agents often fail to recognise that they are done, repeat the same steps or talk past each other; MAST lists step repetition and unawareness of stopping conditions among the most common failures. A stop word depends on an agent remembering to say it, while hard caps on messages, tokens and time end the run regardless. Without them one unattended loop can run up a large bill overnight.

mafail.q: Explain the difference between combining termination conditions with | and with &.
pts: OR stops at the first condition
mafail.model: With |, the run stops as soon as any one condition fires, so each cap is a real limit. With &, it stops only when every condition has fired, so if the stop word is never said the message cap alone will not end it. Safety caps should always be combined with |.

mafail.q: Design stop rules for an overnight coder–reviewer team with a budget per run.
mafail.model: Use one stop word, APPROVED, which the reviewer may say only after the test suite passes. Combine it with message, token and time caps using OR, add a repetition check, and set a spend cap for the whole run. If a cap or the repetition check ends the run, return the last patch marked partial with the stop reason, so an engineer can pick it up in the morning.

subagents.q: In your own words: how do parallel sub-agents with isolated context work, and what do they buy you?
subagents.model: An orchestrator splits a job into pieces that share no inputs and starts one sub-agent per piece at the same time. Each sub-agent works in a fresh context that holds only its brief and its own reading, and sends back a short, structured result instead of its transcript. You gain wall-clock time, since the run takes about as long as the slowest piece plus merging, and breadth, since no single window has to hold everything. You pay in tokens, because every sub-agent carries its own prompt, tools and reasoning.

subagents.q: Your 12 sub-agents finished quickly, but the comparison table contradicts itself. What would you check and change?
pts: pass shared figures in the brief
subagents.model: Contradictions usually mean the pieces were not truly independent: each sub-agent worked out a shared input, such as the USD/INR rate or an API price index, on its own. Compute those figures once in the orchestrator and put them in every brief, make each card record the figure and units it used, and add a merge check at fan-in that flags any card that differs and lists missing companies before the note is written.

subagents.q: How would you choose how many sub-agents to start for a 12-company comparison?
pts: each context must fit its window
coupled work stays with one agent
subagents.model: Start from the window: each sub-agent’s share of filings plus its overhead must fit, so 12 companies at 40k each need at least 3 sub-agents. Beyond that, more sub-agents buy minutes at the price of overhead: in the playground 3 sub-agents cover everything for about ₹244 in 47 minutes, 6 take 27 minutes for ₹292 and 12 take 17 minutes for ₹390. Pick by what a saved minute is worth, respect your provider’s rate limits with a concurrency cap, and keep any coupled step, such as the valuation, with one agent.

cases.title: The alert investigation that takes eighteen minutes
cases.brief: A private bank investigates AML alerts with a single agent that runs four checks in sequence - transaction pattern, counterparty screening, source-of-funds documents, and prior case history - then writes an investigation note. The note follows a fixed template, an analyst makes the final decision, and no customer ever talks to the system. The pilot missed its time target badly and, on a few alerts, produced nothing at all.
evidence: The four checks share no inputs. Each takes 20-40 tool calls and four to five minutes, and the single agent's context reaches about 180k tokens by the end.
Each alert takes 18 minutes against a target of under 6. The budget is ₹40 per alert; the sequential agent spends about ₹9 in tokens.
In the pilot, 7% of alerts ran past 60 agent turns without producing a note. There was no turn cap and no spend cap.
Two checks independently re-derived the same customer profile, and each worker returned its full transcript to the orchestrator, refilling the context the split was meant to protect.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.whenmulti: Start here, and the answer happens to be yes - which is why it is worth being explicit about the test. Four checks sharing no inputs, each filling a context, with a deadline that saved minutes genuinely buy: that is the narrow set of conditions where splitting is right. Note what you are buying - parallelism saves wall-clock time, not tokens, and the ₹40 budget is what makes that trade affordable.
why.supervisor: The shape follows from the split: one orchestrator writes four precise briefs, four workers run their own tool sets and permissions, and the orchestrator assembles the note. The briefs are the whole job - vague ones are why two workers re-derived the same profile - and workers must return findings, not transcripts.
why.mafail: 7% of alerts producing nothing after 60 turns, with no cap of any kind, is an unattended team with no brakes. Set turn and spend caps per run and per day, combine them so that any one firing stops the run rather than requiring all of them, and never accept a “done” claim without checking the note exists.
why.sharedstate: Useful and close to essential: findings belong in a structured store with a reducer per key so four parallel writers cannot overwrite each other, and so every claim in the note carries its source - which an AML file needs anyway. Free-text chat between agents buries findings and loses provenance.
why.subagents: Useful as the mechanism for the fan-out: isolated contexts are what keep 180k tokens from reassembling in one window. Watch the two traps in this very evidence - re-deriving a shared input, and awaiting workers one at a time, which quietly makes a fan-out sequential.
why.handoffs: Not needed: nobody owns this conversation, because there is no conversation. Handoffs move ownership of a dialogue between specialists, and here an analyst makes the decision from a templated note.
why.debate: Not needed on this evidence: the checks are independent evidence-gathering, not a contested judgement, and the final call is a human's. Rounds of debate would multiply an already-failing 18 minutes to argue about facts nobody disputes.

firstWhy.supervisor: Right shape, and you will build exactly this. But reaching for the orchestrator before stating the test is how teams end up splitting coupled work: write down why these four checks qualify, because the next workflow someone wants to parallelise will not, and this decision is the precedent.
firstWhy.mafail: Strong instinct - 7% of alerts silently producing nothing is the kind of failure that gets a pilot cancelled - and the caps are an afternoon's work, so put them in this week regardless. As an ordering choice, though, you would be bounding the sequential agent you are about to replace, and the caps that matter are the ones around the fan-out.
firstWhy.sharedstate: This is the fix for the duplicated profile and for provenance the AML file needs anyway, so it is not wrong. It is just that shared state is where workers put findings, and the workers do not exist yet.

cases.model: Start by stating the test and confirming it passes: four checks that share no inputs, each consuming a context of its own, against a six-minute target with a ₹40 budget that makes extra tokens affordable. That is what justifies a split, and it is worth writing down because parallelism buys time, not tokens. Then build supervisor and workers: one orchestrator issuing four precise, non-overlapping briefs, each worker with its own tools and permissions, each returning structured findings rather than a transcript, and the orchestrator assembling the templated note. Next, put coordination control around it - turn and spend caps per run and per day, wired so any single cap firing halts the run, plus a check that a note actually exists before a run is called done, which is what the 7% needs. Keep findings in shared state with a reducer per key so parallel writers cannot clobber each other and every claim in the note keeps its source. Handoffs and debate have no place here: there is no conversation to own, and the analyst makes the judgement from undisputed facts.
cases.note: The split was right here because the four checks were genuinely independent and the deadline was worth tokens. Case 2 has three specialists that probably should not have been separate agents at all, and Case 3 is where debate earns its cost - so the lesson is the test, not the answer.

whenmulti: Before anything else, symptoms 1 and 2 are asking a question rather than describing a bug: four checks that share no inputs, each filling a context, 18 minutes against a 6-minute target, and a budget with room in it. What decision is this evidence actually setting up?
There is a prior question to all the mechanics - whether this work should be divided between agents at all - and it has a short list of conditions. Check what you gain and what you do not.
Single vs Multi-Agent. Read the pitfall about parallelism saving time rather than tokens, and the one about splitting coupled work.
supervisor: Symptom 4: two workers independently re-derived the same customer profile, and each returned its full transcript to whatever assembled the note. Who was supposed to prevent both of those?

One agent divides the job and puts it back together. The quality of what it writes in each brief decides whether the parts overlap, and what the parts send back decides whether its own context survives.
Supervisor and Workers. The first two pitfalls are symptom 4 exactly: vague briefs causing duplication, and full transcripts flooding the orchestrator.
mafail: Symptom 3: 7% of alerts ran past 60 turns and produced no note, with no turn cap and no spend cap anywhere. This runs unattended. What is missing?
Limits, and a definition of finished that is checked rather than claimed. There is a subtlety in how multiple limits are combined that is worth reading carefully.
Failure Modes and Coordination Control. Note the pitfall about combining caps with AND, and the one about a done claim with no check.

drop.handoffs: Handoffs decide who owns the conversation now. Read the brief: who is having a conversation with this system?
drop.debate: Debate helps on high-stakes answers where a checkable argument can be contested. Are these four checks arguing about a judgement, or gathering independent facts for a human to judge?

cases.firstHint: You have the right pieces and the right shape. Now notice that one item on your list is not a mechanism but a decision - and that writing it down is what stops the next team from splitting work that is coupled.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Whether to split at all decides the shape of everything else, and the conditions that justify it here will not hold for the next workflow.
7% of alerts silently produce no note, which is the failure most likely to get the pilot cancelled.
18 minutes against a 6-minute target is the headline miss, so latency is what the redesign must attack.
whyFirst.why: Order from the decision that constrains the others. The caps matter and should go in this week, and latency is the reason the project exists, but both of those are properties of an architecture you have not committed to yet. Making the independence test explicit is what makes the split defensible here and refusable next time, when somebody proposes four agents for work whose parts talk to each other.

cases.title: The support bot that passes you around
cases.brief: A bank's chat support runs three specialist agents - cards, loans and fraud - each with its own tools and permissions, with a router at the front and peer-to-peer handoffs between them. Customers describe being passed around, the abandonment rate is climbing, and one overnight chat turned into a finance question.
evidence: The three specialists' descriptions overlap heavily, and 23% of chats are routed to the wrong one - often twice in the same conversation.
Nothing travels with a handover. Customers re-explain their problem an average of 2.4 times per chat, and the transcript before the handover is discarded.
Peer-to-peer handoffs have no limit. 4% of chats ping-pong between cards and fraud until the customer leaves.
The bot runs unattended overnight. One chat looped for 90 minutes and spent ₹2,100 in tokens before anyone noticed; there are no turn or spend caps.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.handoffs: Start here, because three of the four symptoms are this one technique misapplied. Overlapping descriptions cause the 23% misroutes and the ping-pong; carrying no context causes the 2.4 retellings; uncapped peer-to-peer transfer causes the loop. Make the specialist descriptions disjoint and specific, pass the conversation so far with every transfer, and cap how many times ownership can change.
why.mafail: A chat that ran 90 minutes and ₹2,100 unattended is a team with no brakes, and the caps are the cheapest work on this page - put them in this week regardless of ordering. Cap turns and spend per conversation, make any single cap firing end the chat into a human queue, and remember that combining caps with AND means none of them fires.
why.sharedstate: The 2.4 retellings are the user-visible half of something structural: what the customer said lives in a chat log that gets discarded at the boundary. Put the facts of the case - the account, the problem, what has been checked, what was promised - in a structured store the next owner reads, instead of hoping free text survives the transfer.
why.whenmulti: Useful as a question to ask honestly, and here the answer is to keep the split: the three specialists have genuinely different tools and permissions, which is one of the few good reasons for separate agents rather than one agent with more tools. Worth revisiting if the permission boundaries ever converge.
why.supervisor: Useful as an alternative shape: a front agent that owns the conversation throughout and calls specialists as tools removes the handover problem by removing the handover. Consider it if disjoint descriptions do not get the misroutes down, but it is a redesign, not this sprint's fix.
why.debate: Not needed: nothing here is a contested judgement needing several opinions. Three agents deliberating over which of them should handle a blocked card would add cost and latency to a conversation a customer is already abandoning.
why.subagents: Not needed: there is no large body of independent material to fan out across, and one customer with one problem is the opposite of a batch. Isolated parallel contexts solve a problem this system does not have.

firstWhy.mafail: Nearly right, and genuinely urgent - ₹2,100 and 90 minutes unattended is money gone and the caps take an afternoon, so do them this week whatever your order. But caps stop the loop without stopping what causes it: the chat still pings between cards and fraud, it just stops sooner. Tokens are recoverable; fix the generator.
firstWhy.sharedstate: This is the fix for the symptom customers actually complain about, so the instinct is sound. But context survives a handover only as well as the handover is designed, and today 23% of handovers go to the wrong specialist - so you would be carefully delivering the case file to the wrong desk.
firstWhy.whenmulti: The best strategic question on the page, and worth asking out loud. But the three specialists have different tools and permissions, which is the one solid reason to keep them apart, so the answer is probably no change - and re-litigating the architecture leaves all four symptoms live meanwhile.

cases.model: Start with handoffs, because three of the four symptoms are the same technique applied badly: rewrite the specialist descriptions so they are disjoint and specific enough that the router cannot reasonably confuse cards with fraud, attach the conversation so far to every transfer so the customer stops re-explaining, and cap the number of ownership changes per chat with a human queue at the end of the cap. Add coordination control immediately alongside it - turn and spend caps per conversation, any one firing ending the chat rather than all of them having to - since 90 unattended minutes and ₹2,100 is pure loss and the work is trivial. Then move the case facts into shared state - account, problem, checks done, promises made - so the next owner reads a record instead of a discarded chat log. Keep the three specialists as separate agents, because different tools and permissions is a real reason to split; a supervisor that owns the conversation and calls specialists as tools is the fallback if disjoint descriptions do not bring the misroutes down. Debate and parallel sub-agents address nothing here.
cases.note: Case 1 split work that was genuinely independent; here three specialists exist for a reason that only just holds, and most of the damage comes from the seam between them. When agents are talking to each other about one customer, the seam is where the bugs live.

handoffs: Symptoms 1, 2 and 3 are one technique going wrong three ways: the specialists' descriptions overlap so 23% of chats go to the wrong one, nothing travels with a transfer so customers repeat themselves, and transfers between peers have no limit so 4% ping-pong. What single mechanism is all of that?
The question is who owns this conversation now - how that owner is chosen, what they are given when they take over, and how many times ownership is allowed to change.
Handoffs. All three pitfalls are in this evidence: overlapping descriptions, passing no context, and uncapped peer-to-peer loops.
mafail: Symptom 4: unattended overnight, one chat looping 90 minutes and ₹2,100, no turn cap and no spend cap. What does any agent team running without a human watching need?
Limits per run and per day, and care about how several limits combine - there is a specific mistake that makes a set of caps fire never instead of early.
Failure Modes and Coordination Control. Read the pitfall about combining caps with AND, and the one about caps set too tight.
sharedstate: Symptom 2 again, from a different angle: customers re-explain their problem 2.4 times, and the transcript before the handover is thrown away. Where should the facts of a case live so that a change of owner does not lose them?
Not in the messages between agents. In something structured that each owner reads and writes, so findings and promises are not buried in free text.
Shared State vs Message Passing. Note the pitfall about free-text chat burying findings and dropping sources.

drop.debate: Debate and critic ensembles earn their cost on high-stakes answers with a contestable argument. What is being argued about when a customer reports a blocked card?
drop.subagents: Parallel sub-agents with isolated contexts suit many independent items compared at once. How many independent items is one customer with one problem?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now ask which symptom causes the others: the loop, the retelling and the misroute are not three faults - two of them are consequences of the first, and one technique governs all three.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: An unattended chat burned ₹2,100 in 90 minutes, and spend with no cap is the only symptom that costs real money.
Three of the four symptoms are the same mechanism misapplied, so one fix addresses the misroutes, the retelling and the ping-pong together.
Customers re-explain their problem 2.4 times per chat, which is the complaint driving the rising abandonment rate.
whyFirst.why: Order by cause. The caps are cheap, urgent and should go in the same week - but they bound the loop rather than remove it, and a token spend is recoverable in a way a misrouted fraud case is not. Overlapping descriptions, empty transfers and uncapped ownership changes are one technique done badly, and fixing it moves three symptoms at once.

cases.title: The denial that one agent decided alone
cases.brief: A health insurer adjudicates complex hospitalisation claims against policy wording. One agent reads the whole file - discharge summary, itemised bills, pre-authorisation, the 60-page policy wording, exclusions, past claims - and either approves, queries or denies. It runs unattended in batches, and a human adjudicator signs off approvals but not denials. An internal audit of denials has just come back badly.
evidence: A claim needs fourteen independent document reviews that together overflow one context window. Today one agent reads them in sequence and runs out of room before the exclusions.
A prototype fan-out had each reviewer re-read the 60-page policy wording from scratch, duplicating the work and twice reaching conflicting readings of the same clause.
On the 9% of claims that are denied, one agent's reading of the exclusion clause is final. The audit found roughly one in six denials was not supported by the wording.
In the prototype, reviewers were awaited one at a time in a loop, so the fan-out ran sequentially, and each returned its full transcript to the assembler.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.subagents: Start here, because symptom 1 is a hard limit rather than a preference: fourteen reviews that together do not fit in one window mean the current design cannot finish, and it is running out of room precisely before the exclusions that the audit is about. Fan the reviews out into isolated contexts - and fix the two traps the prototype already hit, awaiting them concurrently rather than one at a time, and returning findings rather than transcripts.
why.sharedstate: The duplicated policy reading and the two conflicting readings of one clause are what happens when a shared input is re-derived by every worker. Read and structure the policy wording once into shared state with the clause as the key, let reviewers read it rather than re-interpret it, and give each finding a reducer and a source so parallel writes neither clobber each other nor lose provenance.
why.debate: This is the case where more opinions genuinely pay. A denial is high-stakes, the argument is checkable against the wording, and one in six is unsupported - so put contested denials through independent readings and treat disagreement as the escalation signal rather than something to average away. Use independent readings rather than a round of chat, because correlated agents agree on the same mistake and a confident peer pulls the others along.
why.whenmulti: Useful to state, though the evidence has largely settled it: fourteen independent reviews that overflow one window is the clearest case for splitting there is. Worth writing down anyway, so the next team can tell this apart from work whose parts are coupled.
why.supervisor: Useful as the assembly shape: something has to write the fourteen briefs, collect structured findings and reconcile them into a decision. Secondary only because the prototype's failures were in isolation and shared input rather than in the orchestration itself.
why.handoffs: Not needed: there is no conversation and no owner to transfer. Batch adjudication of a document file is the opposite of a dialogue changing hands.
why.mafail: Not needed against these four symptoms, which is a narrower claim than it sounds: the fan-out is a fixed fourteen reviews per claim with a human in the loop, so there is no peer-to-peer loop to break or unbounded spawn to bound. Add a per-claim spend cap when this goes to production, but it fixes nothing the audit found.

firstWhy.sharedstate: Exactly right about the cause of symptom 2, and it is your second step. But shared state is where parallel reviewers read a common input and deposit findings, and today there are no parallel reviewers - one agent reads in sequence until it runs out of window. Build the fan-out, then stop it duplicating work.
firstWhy.debate: This is what the audit is asking for and the most important outcome on the page, so wanting it first is defensible. But a second and third reading of the exclusion clause is worth having only if the reader got as far as the exclusions, and today the context runs out before them. Make the reading possible, then make it contested.
firstWhy.supervisor: The right assembly shape and you will need it. It is also the part the prototype got least wrong: its failures were re-derived inputs and a fan-out that was secretly sequential, both of which sit inside the workers rather than in the orchestration.

cases.model: Start with parallel sub-agents in isolated contexts, because fourteen reviews that together overflow one window is a limit rather than an inefficiency - and the current agent runs out of room just before the exclusions the audit is about. Fan them out, await them concurrently instead of one at a time, and have each return structured findings rather than a transcript. Next, read and structure the 60-page policy wording once into shared state keyed by clause, so reviewers consult one interpretation instead of fourteen, with a reducer per key so parallel writes do not overwrite each other and every finding carries its source - which a claim file needs anyway. Then add debate where it earns its cost: route contested denials to independent readings of the exclusion clause, keep the readings independent rather than conversational so a confident peer cannot pull the others along, and treat disagreement as the signal to escalate to a human rather than something to resolve by majority. Wrap it in a supervisor that writes the briefs and reconciles findings into a decision. Handoffs are meaningless without a conversation, and coordination caps are worth adding in production but address none of the audit's findings.
cases.note: Debate was the wrong answer in both earlier cases and is the right one here, for three specific reasons: the stakes are high, the argument is checkable against a document, and disagreement is useful on its own as an escalation signal. Those three conditions, not the word “important”, are what justify paying for more opinions.

subagents: Symptom 1 is not a preference, it is a wall: fourteen independent document reviews that together do not fit in one context window, read in sequence until the agent runs out of room before the exclusions. What lets many pieces be worked at once without any one context holding all of them?
Run the pieces separately, each with its own window, and bring back only what each concluded. Symptom 4 shows you two ways to get this wrong.
Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context. Read all three pitfalls - re-derived shared input, returned transcripts, and awaiting one by one, which is symptom 4 exactly.
sharedstate: Symptom 2: every reviewer re-read the same 60-page policy wording from scratch, and two of them reached different readings of one clause. What should happen to an input that all of them need?
Interpret it once and put it somewhere they all read, rather than letting each derive it - and think about what happens when several of them write findings at the same time.
Shared State vs Message Passing. Note the pitfall about a key with no reducer losing parallel writes, and the one about everyone reading everything.
debate: Symptom 3: on denials, one agent's reading of an exclusion clause is final, and the audit found about one in six unsupported by the wording. High stakes, and an argument that can be checked against a document. What is that the textbook case for?
More than one opinion - but the value is as much in the disagreement as in the verdict, because disagreement tells you which cases a person should see. Keep the opinions from influencing each other.
Debate and Critic Ensembles. Read the pitfalls about correlated agents and conformity to a confident peer - they decide how you structure it.

drop.handoffs: Handoffs transfer ownership of a conversation between specialists. Which conversation is taking place in a batch adjudication of a document file?
drop.mafail: Coordination control bounds teams that can loop, stall or overspend. With a fixed fourteen reviews per claim and a human adjudicator, what here could loop - and would a cap have prevented any of the audit's findings?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right and they stack in a specific order. Ask what has to be physically possible before the other two matter: the audit is about the exclusion clause, and today the agent never reaches it.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Fourteen reviews overflow one window, so the agent never reaches the exclusions that every other fix is about.
One in six denials is unsupported by the policy wording, which is the finding the audit actually raised.
Re-reading the 60-page wording fourteen times is the largest duplicated cost in the prototype.
whyFirst.why: Order by what is possible before what is desirable. The unsupported denials are the reason this work exists, and contested readings are how you fix them - but a second opinion on a clause nobody read is worth nothing, and the current design runs out of context before the exclusions every time. Make the whole file readable, share the wording once, then argue about it.

whenmulti.t: A job has 6 independent subtasks of 5 minutes each and a chat-equivalent baseline of 3k tokens per subtask. One agent uses about 4× the baseline; six sub-agents use about 15× and need 2 minutes to merge. How many extra tokens (in thousands) does the multi-agent design use?
whenmulti.a: Baseline: 6 × 3k = 18k. Single agent: 4 × 18k = 72k tokens and 30 minutes. Multi-agent: 15 × 18k = 270k tokens and 5 + 2 = 7 minutes. Extra tokens: 270k − 72k = 198k, bought to save 23 minutes.
iv: When would you choose a single agent even though the task has many steps?

When the steps share context or make coupled decisions, such as editing one codebase or building one valuation model. Split agents make implicit decisions that can conflict. A single agent with context compression is cheaper and more coherent.
How do you estimate whether multi-agent is worth it before building it?

Draw the task graph, count branches that share no inputs, and check each fits one context window. Estimate tokens (roughly 15× chat for multi-agent against 4× for one agent) and wall time (slowest branch plus merge). Split only if the time or coverage gained is worth more than the extra tokens.
mis: Don’t split a task because it has many steps.
Split only when steps are independent and each fits its own context window.
Don’t assume parallel agents save tokens.
Budget for more tokens: parallelism saves wall time, not tokens.

supervisor.t: An orchestrator uses 2k tokens of its own and sends out 6 workers. Each worker reads 25k tokens and returns a 1.5k summary. How many tokens does the orchestrator’s context hold after collecting summaries (in thousands)?
supervisor.a: 2k of its own + 6 × 1.5k of summaries = 11k tokens. If workers returned full transcripts it would hold 2k + 6 × 25k = 152k, which is why only final messages return.
iv: What must a worker’s brief contain, and why?

An objective, an output format, guidance on which tools and sources to use, and clear boundaries. The worker starts with a fresh context and sees only its own prompt and the brief, so anything missing is simply unknown to it.
How is a supervisor different from a fixed execution graph?
In a graph the steps are fixed in advance by the developer. A supervisor decides at run time how to split the task, how many workers to start and what each should do, then merges what comes back.
mis: Don’t brief a worker with a one-line title.
Give it the objective, output format, sources and limits it needs.
Don’t give every worker every tool.
Scope tools per worker: readers get read-only tools.

handoffs.t: Without handoff payloads, 40% of 1,000 transferred chats make the user repeat details, adding 4 turns each. A typed payload removes the repeats. At 1.5k tokens per turn, how many tokens (in thousands) does the payload save across the 1,000 chats?
handoffs.a: Chats with repeats: 0.4 × 1,000 = 400. Extra turns: 400 × 4 = 1,600. Tokens: 1,600 × 1.5k = 2,400k tokens, or 2.4 million.
iv: When do you use a handoff rather than calling a specialist as a tool?

Use a handoff when the specialist should own the rest of the conversation and answer the user directly. Use agent-as-tool when a manager should keep control, call the specialist for a sub-answer and compose the reply itself.
Why do handoff descriptions matter so much?

Handoffs are exposed to the model as tools, so the triage model chooses among them from their names and descriptions. Overlapping descriptions leave it guessing, which causes misroutes and back-and-forth transfers.
mis: Don’t pass the whole transcript on every handoff.
Pass a small typed payload and filter the history.
Don’t allow unlimited back-handoffs.
Cap turns and hops so two specialists cannot ping-pong.

sharedstate.t: Four agents each write 5 findings of 0.6k tokens to a shared board, and each agent then reads the board. How many tokens (in thousands) does each agent read if it reads everything?
sharedstate.a: 4 × 5 = 20 findings × 0.6k = 12k tokens per agent. If each reads only the 2 fields it needs (say a quarter of the board), that falls to 3k.
iv: What happens in LangGraph when two parallel nodes write the same key?
If the key has no reducer, LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError because it cannot pick one value; sequential writes simply overwrite. With a reducer such as operator.add, the updates are merged.
When would you choose message passing over a shared board?

When agents belong to separate systems or teams, when each should see only what is addressed to it, or when you need an auditable record of who told whom what. Protocols such as A2A standardise those messages across systems.
mis: Don’t leave a multi-writer field without a reducer.
Declare how updates merge, for example Annotated[list, operator.add].
Don’t let every agent read everything.
Scope reads to the fields each agent needs, and record the author and source of every entry.

debate.t: Three agents are each right 70% of the time, with independent errors. What is the majority-vote accuracy, in percent?
debate.a: The vote is right when at least 2 of 3 are right: 3 × 0.7² × 0.3 + 0.7³ = 0.441 + 0.343 = 0.784, so 78.4%. Correlated errors would pull this back towards 70%.
iv: When is multi-agent debate worth its cost?

When agents’ errors are fairly independent, the answer has a checkable argument, and errors are expensive. Measure it against plain majority voting at the same number of calls; recent work finds voting explains most of debate’s gains.
What goes wrong in debate?

Agents conform to a confident but wrong peer, anchor on their first answer (degeneration of thought), or share the same blind spot when they use the same model and prompt. A judge can also be biased when agents use different models.
mis: Don’t take the last speaker’s answer as the result.
Aggregate the final round by majority vote or a judge with a rubric.
Don’t run debate rounds by default.
Start with independent answers and a vote; add rounds only if they measurably help.

mafail.t: A coder–reviewer team uses 4k tokens per message. With OR-combined caps of 30 messages and 100k tokens, after how many messages does the run stop if nothing else stops it?
mafail.a: The token cap is reached at 100k ÷ 4k = 25 messages, before the message cap of 30. With OR, the first cap reached stops the run, so it stops at 25 messages.
iv: Why combine termination conditions with OR rather than AND?
OR stops the run when any one cap is reached, so each cap is a real limit. AND waits until all conditions hold at once, so a run whose agents never say the stop word will never end.
What are the three MAST failure categories?

System design issues (such as step repetition and unawareness of stopping conditions), inter-agent misalignment (such as ignoring another agent’s input or a reasoning–action mismatch) and task verification failures (such as stopping early or skipping checks).
mis: Don’t rely on agents to say when they are done.
Add hard caps on messages, tokens and time, combined with OR.
Don’t accept “done” without a check.
Run a verifier, such as the test suite, and return partial results with a stop reason.

subagents.t: An orchestrator fans out 12 company analyses, one isolated session each, with a concurrency cap of 4. Every session takes 10 minutes. Planning takes 2 minutes and the merge check 3 minutes. What is the wall-clock time, in minutes?
subagents.a: With 4 at a time, the 12 sessions run in 12 ÷ 4 = 3 waves of 10 minutes: 30 minutes. Add 2 for planning and 3 for the merge check: 2 + 30 + 3 = 35 minutes. Run one after another they would take 2 + 120 + 3 = 125 minutes; the token bill is the same either way.
iv: Why should a sub-agent return a condensed card rather than its transcript?

The point of an isolated context is that raw reading stays with the sub-agent. A card of a few hundred tokens with a fixed schema and sources lets the orchestrator hold 12 results in about 6k tokens; 12 transcripts would be hundreds of thousands of tokens, overflow its window and make the merge worse.
Two sub-agents report different USD/INR rates for the same quarter. What went wrong and how do you fix it?

The companies were not truly independent: each sub-agent re-derived a shared input. Compute the shared figures once in the orchestrator and pass them in every brief, record the figure each card used, and run a merge check that flags any card that differs.
mis: Don’t let every sub-agent look up the same shared input.
Compute it once and pass it in the brief; the merge check confirms everyone used it.
Don’t await sub-agents one by one in a loop.
Start them together with gather or a TaskGroup, under a semaphore that caps concurrency.

gloss: orchestrator
The agent that plans a task, sends pieces to worker agents and merges their results.
sub-agent
An agent started by another agent to do one piece of work in its own, fresh context.
context isolation
Keeping each agent’s intermediate reading and tool calls out of other agents’ context windows.
handoff
Transferring ownership of a live conversation from one agent to another, exposed to the model as a tool.
triage agent
The first agent in a support flow; it classifies the request and hands it to a specialist.
blackboard
A shared store that several agents read from and write to, such as a typed graph state.
reducer
A function that says how a new update merges with a state key, for example appending to a list.
provenance
A record of which agent wrote an entry and from which source.
A2A
Agent2Agent, an open protocol for messages and tasks between separate agent systems.
majority vote
Choosing the answer given by more than half of the agents.
degeneration of thought
An agent’s tendency to stick with its first answer even when it is wrong.
termination condition
A rule that ends a multi-agent run, such as a message, token or time cap.
MAST
A taxonomy of 14 multi-agent failure modes in 3 categories, built from over 1,600 traces.
wall time
Elapsed real time from start to finish, as opposed to the total compute or tokens used.
fan-out and fan-in
Starting many independent pieces of work at once, then collecting and combining their results in one step.
condensed return
The short, fixed-format result a sub-agent sends back, such as a card of at most 500 tokens, instead of its full transcript.
merge check
A fan-in step that compares results for shared figures, units, conflicts and gaps before they are combined.
concurrency cap
The maximum number of sub-agents or calls allowed to run at the same time, often enforced with a semaphore.

whenmulti.name: Agent Execution Graphs
whenmulti.note: Execution graphs run independent steps in parallel inside one agent; whenmulti asks whether those branches need separate agents, each with its own context and token bill.

whenmulti.name: CrewAI, AutoGen and Microsoft Agent Framework
whenmulti.note: Choose a multi-agent framework only after checking that the work really needs several agents.

supervisor.name: Agent Execution Graphs
supervisor.note: In an execution graph the steps are fixed in advance; a supervisor decides them at run time.

supervisor.name: Action Policies and Approval Thresholds
supervisor.note: Per-worker tool scopes are least privilege applied to each agent.

supervisor.name: Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context
supervisor.note: Supervisor and Workers covers how the orchestrator briefs and tool-scopes each worker; parallel sub-agents covers running them at once, condensing what returns and checking it at fan-in.

handoffs.name: Model Routing and Tiering
handoffs.note: Routing picks a model for one request; a handoff moves ownership of the conversation, with its state, to another agent.

sharedstate.name: Procedural Memory
sharedstate.note: Procedural memory is one agent’s store; shared state is about concurrent writes and read scopes across several agents.

sharedstate.name: Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context
sharedstate.note: When pieces share inputs, pass them in each brief or through typed shared state with provenance, so the merge check can spot conflicting figures.

debate.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
debate.note: LLM judges grade outputs after the fact; debate produces the answer at run time, and its judge step reuses the same rubric discipline.

mafail.name: Prompt & Tool Controls
mafail.note: Prompt and tool controls trim one agent’s usage; coordination control adds team-level caps on turns, tokens, time and depth.

mafail.name: Agent-as-a-Judge
mafail.note: The verifier that must pass before a team stops plays the agent-as-judge role.

subagents.name: Supervisor and Workers
subagents.note: Supervisor and Workers covers how the orchestrator briefs and tool-scopes each worker; parallel sub-agents covers running them at once, condensing what returns and checking it at fan-in.

subagents.name: Parallel and Sequential Tool Calls
subagents.note: Parallel tool calls run several tools inside one agent's context; parallel sub-agents give each piece its own context, so the raw results never meet.

subagents.name: Context Budgeting
subagents.note: Isolating each piece in its own sub-agent and returning a 500-token card is a context budget enforced by architecture.

subagents.name: Shared State vs Message Passing
subagents.note: When pieces share inputs, pass them in each brief or through typed shared state with provenance, so the merge check can spot conflicting figures.
